Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Resectable (potentially resectable but no factor currently limits resection).  
• Rationale:  
  – Two liver metastases, each ≤3 cm, located in separate, non‑adjacent segments (II and V).  
  – No radiologic evidence of major vascular or biliary invasion reported.  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  – Primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction) and can be addressed surgically; removal of segments II and V would leave a sufficient future liver remnant in a normal liver.  
  – RAS wild‑type status and low tumor burden meet current criteria for curative intent surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Urgent primary tumor control – Perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or left hemicolectomy) to relieve obstruction. Rationale: symptomatic primary lesion is priority; resection eliminates source of complications and provides pathology for grading.  
B. Post‑operative recovery and systemic therapy – After adequate wound healing (≈2 weeks), initiate peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑VEGF). Rationale: standard of care for resectable synchronous liver metastases to treat micrometastatic disease and improve disease‑free survival.  
C. Curative liver resection – Plan a staged or simultaneous hepatic resection of segment II (left lateral segmentectomy) and segment V (segmentectomy or wedge resection). If intra‑operative assessment confirms adequate FLR and no unexpected vascular involvement, a simultaneous colon‑liver operation can be performed; otherwise, schedule liver surgery after completion of chemotherapy. Rationale: both lesions are amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with clear margins while preserving liver function.  
D. Adjuvant follow‑up – Continue surveillance with serial CEA, cross‑sectional imaging, and consider additional systemic therapy based on final pathology (grade, margins, nodal status). Rationale: to detect recurrence early and provide further systemic control if indicated.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance (Minagawa et al.)

Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable but likely resectable after confirmation of hepatic functional reserve).  
- Justification:  
  • Single liver lesion, 2.5 cm, located peripherally in segment VI – meets size and number criteria for hepatic resection.  
  • No radiologic evidence of major vascular (portal or hepatic vein) invasion or biliary involvement reported.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT and FDG‑PET.  
  • Assuming adequate future liver remnant (FLR) – typical for a solitary peripheral lesion in the right liver.  
  • Primary colorectal tumor still present; resection of the colon primary is required before or in conjunction with liver surgery, influencing timing but not the intrinsic resectability of the metastasis.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to confirm lesion characteristics, vascular anatomy, and FLR volume.  
   – Perform colonoscopy with biopsy to grade differentiation and assess obstruction/perforation risk.  
   – Baseline labs (CEA trend, liver function, carcino‑embryonic antigen, KRAS confirmed).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (6 cycles)  
   – Regimen: FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) given KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   – Rationale: Assess tumor biology, potential down‑staging, and treat micrometastatic disease; also allows time to complete staging work‑up and optimize patient’s nutritional/functional status.  

C. Surgical resection (performed after restaging post‑chemotherapy)  
   – Option 1 (preferred if patient is fit): Simultaneous resection – right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis plus anatomical segment VI resection (segmentectomy or wedge) in the same operation.  
   – Option 2 (if concern for operative time or liver quality): Staged approach – first right hemicolectomy, recover 4–6 weeks, then liver resection.  
   – Rationale: Single peripheral metastasis allows limited hepatic resection with low morbidity; simultaneous surgery reduces total hospital stay and avoids delay in oncologic control.  

D. Adjuvant therapy  
   – Resume or complete a total of 12 cycles of systemic chemotherapy (including the neoadjuvant cycles) post‑operatively, adjusting based on pathologic response and tolerance.  
   – Consider enrollment in clinical trial or use of maintenance bevacizumab if indicated.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Single liver metastasis, 1.8 cm, located in segment III – amenable to wedge resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; however, thoraco‑abdominal imaging has not been performed, so distant spread cannot be excluded.  
  • Primary rectal tumor is T3N1 without obstruction, perforation or bleeding, making it suitable for curative‑intent resection after neoadjuvant radiotherapy.  
  • RAS wild‑type status supports use of anti‑EGFR agents if systemic therapy is indicated.  
  • Definitive assessment of vascular involvement, FLR ratio, and extra‑hepatic sites is lacking; therefore the case remains “potentially” rather than definitively resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast.  
   – Rationale: Confirm absence of extra‑hepatic metastases, delineate hepatic vasculature, assess FLR, and verify that the lesion has no major vascular or biliary invasion.  

B. Neoadjuvant treatment of the rectal primary  
   – Deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) followed by a 4‑week interval.  
   – Consider adding systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 4 cycles of FOLFOX) during the interval because of synchronous liver disease and N‑positive status.  
   – Rationale: Improves local control of the rectal tumor, allows down‑staging, and treats micrometastatic disease systemically.  

C. Liver‑directed surgery (simultaneous or staged)  
   – If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a steatotic liver) and no major vascular involvement, plan a simultaneous low anterior resection of the rectum with a non‑anatomical segment III resection (wedge or segmentectomy).  
   – If FLR is marginal or vascular anatomy is unfavorable, perform staged approach: first rectal resection after radiotherapy, then liver resection after recovery.  
   – Rationale: Single small peripheral metastasis can be removed safely; simultaneous resection reduces overall treatment time and hospitalizations when technically feasible.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   – After recovery, administer postoperative chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS wild‑type) for 6 months.  
   – Rationale: Consolidates disease control, addresses potential occult micrometastases, and follows standard guidelines for stage III rectal cancer with synchronous liver metastasis.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
(Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Three hepatic lesions, each ≤3 cm, located in segments IV, V, VI – within the conventional limits for hepatic resection (≤4 lesions, each ≤5 cm).  
  • Imaging shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no definite vascular invasion, allowing a safe anatomical resection (right hepatectomy or combined segment IV + right anterior resection).  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease on available imaging; however, thoracic imaging and comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging are missing, which is required to confirm true absence of metastases.  
  • FLR (future liver remnant) volumetry has not been reported; adequacy of the left lateral sector (segments II‑III) must be confirmed, especially in a 72‑year‑old patient.  
  • Primary colorectal tumor has not been reported as resected; simultaneous or staged resection will influence operative planning.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging  
   – Obtain a thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary, osseous, or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Perform liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate FLR ratio; if FLR < 30‑35 % in a normal liver, consider portal vein embolization.  
   – Endoscopic evaluation of the transverse colon lesion to assess resectability and need for pre‑operative bowel preparation.  

B. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) or triplet (FOLFOXIRI) chemotherapy, adding anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) given KRAS mutation and high CEA, to:  
     • Treat occult micrometastatic disease,  
     • Assess tumor biology (response), and  
     • Potentially downsize hepatic lesions.  

C. Restaging after induction  
   – Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and repeat thoraco‑abdominal imaging.  
   – Re‑evaluate FLR; if still insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization and allow hypertrophy (4‑6 weeks).  

D. Surgical phase (once resectability confirmed)  
   – If patient’s performance status permits, perform simultaneous resection:  
     • Segmental colectomy (laparoscopic or open) of the transverse colon primary with oncologic lymphadenectomy,  
     • Anatomical right hepatectomy (segments V‑VIII) plus segment IV resection, preserving left lateral sector (II‑III) as FLR.  
   – If simultaneous approach is deemed high risk (e.g., borderline FLR, comorbidities), stage the procedures: first colorectal resection, recover, then liver resection after induction therapy.  

E. Adjuvant therapy  
   – Resume or continue systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative treatment, adjusting based on pathological response and postoperative recovery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable pending confirmation of adequate future liver remnant).  
- Rationale:  
  • Four liver metastases, each ≤3 cm, located peripherally in segments II, III, V, and VIII with no vascular or biliary invasion.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on available imaging.  
  • Primary tumor is T3N1, amenable to curative resection.  
  • According to current hepatobiliary oncology criteria, ≤4 lesions ≤5 cm without major vascular involvement are considered resectable provided the FLR is sufficient; the FLR assessment is missing, therefore the case is deemed “potentially” resectable until that data is confirmed.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging – Obtain thoracic CT, liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, and assess performance status, comorbidities, and calculate FLR (CT volumetry). Rationale: complete staging is required to confirm absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease and to verify that the FLR will support resection.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – Initiate 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS‑wild‑type status. Rationale: systemic therapy assesses tumor biology, may further downsize liver lesions, and treats micrometastatic disease; it also allows time to complete staging work‑up.  

C. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy – Repeat liver MRI and chest CT to evaluate response and re‑measure FLR. If disease remains resectable and FLR is adequate, proceed to surgery. Rationale: ensures that no progression has occurred and that liver reserve is sufficient.  

D. Simultaneous curative resection – Perform a segmental colectomy (sigmoid resection with oncologic lymphadenectomy) combined with a parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (wedge or segmentectomy of lesions in segments II, III, V, VIII) aiming for R0 margins while preserving at least 25–30 % FLR in a non‑cirrhotic liver. Rationale: simultaneous surgery is safe in fit patients when liver resections are limited and can reduce overall treatment time.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (including any postoperative cycles needed to reach the planned duration). Rationale: consolidates systemic control and follows guideline‑recommended total chemotherapy exposure for stage III colon cancer with synchronous metastases.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• The patient is potentially resectable.  
  – Liver disease: 2 metastases, each ≤4 cm, located in segments II and IVa; middle hepatic vein is preserved, no reported major vascular or biliary invasion, and no extra‑hepatic disease on imaging.  
  – Primary tumor: T4N2 colon cancer, not yet resected; technically resectable but requires oncologic resection (right hemicolectomy ± en‑bloc resection of involved adjacent structures).  
  – Oncologic criteria (≤4 liver lesions, each ≤5 cm, adequate future liver remnant, no uncontrolled extra‑hepatic disease) are met, but confirmation of FLR volume, vascular involvement, and patient fitness is still required; therefore the case is classified as potentially resectable rather than outright resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Phase A – Primary tumor control  
   – Perform a right hemicolectomy (with en‑bloc resection of any adjacent organ if T4 invasion is confirmed).  
   – Rationale: the MDT prioritized control of the primary; resection prevents obstruction, perforation, or bleeding and provides pathologic staging.

B. Phase B – Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   – After postoperative recovery, initiate 6 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
   – Rationale: systemic therapy addresses micrometastatic disease, may down‑size liver lesions, and serves as a biologic test of tumor behavior.

C. Phase C – Restaging and functional assessment  
   – Repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and volumetric CT to assess response of liver metastases and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
   – Rationale: ensures that liver resection remains feasible and that an adequate FLR (≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected) is present.

D. Phase D – Curative liver resection  
   – Perform parenchyma‑sparing anatomical resection of segments II and IVa, preserving the middle hepatic vein, aiming for R0 margins.  
   – Rationale: curative intent for hepatic disease; preserving the middle hepatic vein maximizes FLR and reduces postoperative liver insufficiency.  
   – If intra‑operative assessment shows sufficient liver reserve and the patient’s condition permits, a simultaneous colon and liver resection could be considered, but a staged approach is preferred given the T4 primary.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.
• Given the high CEA level (95 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Assess potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel, duodenum)
• 3 options
-	Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis, first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications.
-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.
-	Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Liver surgery after restaging
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan restaging.
• If tumor response is observed on primary cancer : proceed to oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis
• If tumor response is observed on liver metastases, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment II wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy.
• If stability or progression is observed, proceed to anatomic left hepatectomy preserving the middle hepatic vein guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (requires confirmation of a sufficient future liver remnant and absence of major vascular or biliary invasion).  
- Justification:  
  • Number of hepatic lesions = 3 (≤5) and each ≤2 cm (≤5 cm).  
  • All lesions are confined to segments VI‑VIII, allowing an anatomic right posterior sectorectomy or non‑anatomic wedge resections with preservation of left liver.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on PET (lungs, peritoneum, nodes, bone negative).  
  • RAS wild‑type and CEA 60 ng/mL do not preclude resection.  
  • Missing data that could downgrade resectability: FLR volume/ratio, presence of portal/hepatic vein contact, liver function tests, and detailed arterial anatomy.

   – Initiate 3–6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX) ± anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) given KRAS‑mutated, high‑risk disease.  
   – Rationale: down‑size liver lesions, treat occult micrometastases, and assess tumor biology (response).  

C. Primary tumor management  
   – Perform oncologic resection of the left‑sided colon cancer (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy) either before or simultaneously with liver surgery, depending on response to chemotherapy and patient fitness.  
   – Rationale: T4aN2 disease mandates curative resection; simultaneous resection can be considered if operative risk acceptable and liver disease remains resectable.  

D. Re‑assessment after neoadjuvant therapy  
   – Repeat imaging (MRI, CT) to evaluate lesion size, vascular involvement, and FLR.  
   – If FLR insufficient, consider portal vein embolization or two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   – Rationale: ensure R0 liver resection with adequate postoperative liver function.  

E. Curative liver resection  
   – Perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy targeting segments IV, V, and VIII, aiming for negative margins (R0).  
   – Rationale: limited number and size of lesions allow anatomic or non‑anatomic resections while preserving liver parenchyma.  

F. Adjuvant therapy  
   – Continue postoperative chemotherapy to complete a total of 6–12 months of systemic treatment, tailored to response and pathology.  
   – Rationale: high‑risk primary (T4aN2) and KRAS mutation warrant systemic control.

Case_Content:
Man, 49 years old, T2N0 rectal tumor associated with a single 2.8 cm liver metastasis in segment V at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Single metastasis, resectable upfront, surgery considered after local treatment of the primary.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Single liver lesion, 2.8 cm, located in peripheral segment V, which is amenable to an anatomic segmentectomy or wedge resection with clear margins.  
  • No reported vascular, biliary, or portal invasion; absence of these high‑risk features supports technical resectability.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease on available imaging; thoraco‑abdominal CT of the abdomen performed and thoracic CT not performed – pending confirmation, extra‑hepatic spread is assumed absent.  
  • Primary rectal tumor is T2N0, resectable with standard oncologic technique; therefore the overall disease burden is limited and can be addressed surgically in a staged or combined approach.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Staging and baseline work‑up  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult pulmonary metastases.  
   – Perform liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate lesion anatomy, vascular relationships, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
   – Complete molecular profiling (RAS/RAF, MSI) beyond KRAS to guide systemic therapy.  

B. Neoadjuvant treatment of the rectal primary  
   – Deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiotherapy depending on distance from anal verge and sphincter considerations.  
   – Rationale: Improves local control, down‑stages the tumor, and aligns timing with hepatic management.  

C. Surgical resection of the primary tumor  
   – Perform low anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving procedure) 6–8 weeks after completion of radiotherapy, provided the patient is fit and no progression is noted on restaging.  

D. Restaging and peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Re‑image liver (MRI) and chest (CT) after primary resection to confirm unchanged hepatic disease and absence of extra‑hepatic lesions.  
   – If disease remains limited, consider peri‑operative (neoadjuvant or adjuvant) FOLFOX/XELOX chemotherapy for 2–3 cycles to address micrometastatic risk, especially given KRAS mutation.  

E. Hepatic resection  
   – Proceed with a segment V anatomical resection or non‑anatomic wedge excision with negative margins (R0).  
   – Ensure FLR ≥ 20 % in a healthy liver; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and vascular anatomy.  
   – Rationale: Curative intent resection of solitary metastasis offers the best long‑term survival.  

F. Post‑operative surveillance  
   – Serial CEA measurements and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution pelvic MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm primary tumor location, circumferential and distal margins, lymph nodes involvement, invasion of fascia recti. 

B. Systemic therapy

• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T2N0 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy (combined approach preferred)
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single lesion <3cm using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment V metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment V metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor

– Parenchymal-sparing segment II wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• This combined approach avoids multiple surgeries and is safe for a solitary peripheral metastasis.
• Alternative : staged atypical resection of the single metastasis followed after recovery with oncologic low anterior resection with TME principles

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (conversion‑resectable).  
- Justification:  
  • Seven liver metastases are bilobar, exceeding the usual criteria for upfront resection (≥4 lesions, bilobar distribution).  
  • One lesion shows vascular contact with the right portal branch, raising concern for portal involvement but not yet proven invasion.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, hepatic arterial anatomy, or biliary involvement; therefore a definitive “resectable” status cannot be assigned at this time.  
  • Absence of extra‑hepatic disease on current imaging supports the possibility of achieving an R0 liver resection after down‑staging.  
  • Consequently, the disease is deemed unresectable upfront but potentially resectable after effective conversion chemotherapy and reassessment of FLR.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion therapy – Initiate FOLFOX + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents). Rationale: aim to achieve tumor shrinkage, convert liver disease to resectable status, and treat occult micrometastases.  
B. Restaging after 3–4 months – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT chest/abdomen. Assess:  
   – Response of hepatic lesions (size reduction, loss of vascular contact).  
   – FLR volume calculation; if FLR < 30 % in a normal liver, plan portal vein embolization (PVE).  
   – Status of the primary colon tumor (size, local invasion, symptomatology).  
   Rationale: objective imaging determines whether curative liver surgery is feasible and whether additional hepatic hypertrophy maneuvers are needed.  
C. Surgical phase – If restaging shows adequate tumor response and sufficient FLR:  
   – Option 1 (simultaneous approach): Perform right hemicolectomy (or extended right colectomy) together with staged or combined liver metastasectomy (e.g., two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS if FLR remains marginal).  
   – Option 2 (sequential approach): First resect the colon primary (if symptomatic or if oncologic timing favours), followed by liver resection after a short interval (2–4 weeks).  
   Rationale: simultaneous resection reduces total operative time and hospital stay when both procedures are technically feasible; sequential resection is chosen when liver surgery would be extensive or when primary tumor symptoms dictate priority.  
D. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Resume/continue postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for a total of 6‑12 months, tailored to pathologic response and patient tolerance. Rationale: consolidates disease control and addresses microscopic residual disease.  
E. Surveillance – Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually. Rationale: early detection of recurrence permits timely salvage interventions.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven bilobar liver metastases (1–4 cm) associated with vascular contact with the right portal branch and no reported extrahepatic disease. The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and portal contact make a complete R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant unlikely with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (520 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX + bevacizumab.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, separation from portal structures, and reduction in the number/volume of lesions to achieve secondary resectability.

C. Early and repeated radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response, particularly the relationship of lesions to the right portal branch and overall liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA dynamics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Consider surgery if chemotherapy induces:
– Reduction in lesion size and number allowing parenchymal-sparing resections or staged hepatectomy or combined resection and ablation.
– Clearance from portal structures.
– Feasibility of achieving R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern and tumor location.
• Portal vein embolization may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If no adequate response
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T3N1M1 sigmoid tumor, four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with one in contact with the right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 240 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar involvement for conversion, imaging to be re-evaluated after 4 cycles of chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (conversion‑eligible).  
• Rationale: • Four bilobar metastases without documented extra‑hepatic disease meet typical criteria for hepatic clearance if an R0 resection can be achieved and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) is preserved. • One lesion contacts the right hepatic vein; vascular involvement can be managed with careful dissection or reconstruction in experienced centers. • RAS wild‑type status and high CEA suggest biologic aggressiveness but also predict responsiveness to modern conversion chemotherapy. • Current lack of FLR volumetry, lesion dimensions, and response to systemic therapy precludes a definitive “resectable” label; therefore the case is deemed potentially resectable pending down‑staging and detailed hepatic volumetric assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 4–6 cycles.  
   – Rationale: Aim to achieve tumor shrinkage, increase the chance of R0 resection, and allow assessment of tumor biology.  

B. Perform restaging after chemotherapy: high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging, hepatic volumetry, and CT‑based portal venous anatomy assessment.  
   – Rationale: Determine lesion response, exact size, relationship to vascular structures, and calculate FLR; essential for surgical planning.  

C. If restaging shows ≥30 % reduction of tumor burden and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % after chemotherapy) with clear vascular margins, proceed to hepatic surgery.  
   – Option 1 (simultaneous approach): If the sigmoid primary is resectable and the patient is fit, perform sigmoid colectomy with curative‑intent liver resection in the same operation (parenchymal‑sparing resections, possible right hepatic vein reconstruction).  
   – Option 2 (staged approach): If the primary tumor is large, symptomatic, or requires a complex resection, first perform sigmoid colectomy, then after recovery (2–3 weeks) undertake liver surgery; consider portal vein embolization or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS if FLR is insufficient.  

D. Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or transition to maintenance) for 3–6 months.  
   – Rationale: Consolidate response, eradicate microscopic disease, and improve disease‑free survival.

According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely resectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all 4 lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (240 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• The objective is tumor downsizing, separation from the right hepatic vein, and reduction of bilobar tumor burden to enable secondary resectability.

C. Early radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after 4 cycles as planned to reassess:
– Relationship of the segment VIII lesion to the right hepatic vein.
– Global tumor response and potential for parenchymal-sparing resections.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered if imaging shows:
– Clearance from the right hepatic vein.
– Feasibility of multiple parenchymal-sparing resections or a staged hepatectomy.
– Adequate future liver remnant after planned resections.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Combined parenchymal-sparing resections of segments II, III, VI, and VIII.
• If necessary, a two-stage hepatectomy strategy depending on response pattern and FLR considerations.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥8 lesions), maximum size 4.5 cm, partial contact with the IVC at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 890 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, potentially resectable after major response to FOLFOXIRI.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (conversion‑resectable)  
- Rationale:  
  • Multiple liver metastases (≥8) with a largest diameter of 4.5 cm exceed the usual criteria for immediate “resectable” disease, but the MDT reports a major response to FOLFOXIRI, suggesting down‑staging is feasible.  
  • Partial contact with the IVC represents vascular involvement that may be addressed with vascular resection/reconstruction or by ablative techniques; it does not automatically preclude resection.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; however, definitive staging of the chest, bone and other sites is lacking, and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) has not been quantified.  
  • Therefore, resection is possible after further assessment of response, FLR, and exclusion of extra‑hepatic metastases, placing the case in the “potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continuation of systemic therapy (conversion chemotherapy)  
   - Maintain or intensify the current FOLFOXIRI regimen (consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy if RAS wild‑type) until maximal radiologic response is achieved (typically 3–6 months).  
   - Rationale: To further shrink tumor burden, increase the chance of achieving R0 margins, and potentially convert borderline lesions away from vascular structures.

B. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, volumetric CT for FLR calculation, and full thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) plus bone scan to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Rationale: Precise mapping of lesion number, segmental distribution, vascular anatomy, and confirmation of disease limited to the liver are prerequisites for surgical planning.

C. Pre‑operative liver preparation  
   - If FLR is <30 % (or <40 % after extensive chemotherapy), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
   - Rationale: Ensuring an adequate FLR reduces postoperative liver failure risk.

D. Surgical management  
   1. Primary colon tumor – If not yet resected and the patient is asymptomatic, plan a staged approach: resect the primary after liver surgery or simultaneously if intra‑operative assessment deems it safe.  
   2. Liver metastases – Aim for an R0, parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy; employ vascular control techniques for the IVC‑contacting lesion (e.g., IVC patch, cavectomy with reconstruction, or adjunctive ablation). Consider intra‑operative ultrasound to identify additional lesions.  
   - Rationale: Curative intent requires complete removal of all hepatic disease while preserving sufficient functional liver tissue.

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months, with consideration of targeted agents based on molecular profile.  
   - Rationale: To eradicate microscopic residual disease and reduce recurrence risk.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with extensive bilobar liver metastases (≥8 lesions, up to 4.5 cm) with partial contact with the inferior vena cava and no reported extrahepatic disease. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and caval contact make a complete R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant not feasible with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront, with a possibility of secondary resectability only after major tumor response.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (890 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type and MSS status do not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Preoperative portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy is needed.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Woman, 52 years old, T3N2 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with bilobar liver metastases (six lesions, 2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 600 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: invasion of the middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, goal of volumetric reduction with chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Six bilobar hepatic lesions (2–5 cm) exceed the ideal “≤3 lesions ≤3 cm” criteria for straightforward resection.  
  • Invasion of the middle hepatic vein represents major vascular involvement that may preclude an R0 liver‑only resection without vascular reconstruction or staged hypertrophy.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT, supporting a curative intent if hepatic disease can be cleared.  
  • High CEA (600 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive biology, reinforcing the need for down‑staging.  
  • Because the MDT already judged the disease “not initially resectable” and proposed volumetric reduction, the case fits the definition of borderline/potentially resectable disease that may become resectable after systemic therapy and/or portal vein embolization.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  

A. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6–8 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab).  
   – Rationale: Aim to achieve tumor shrinkage, convert liver disease to resectable status, and treat micrometastatic rectal disease. KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.

B. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary (long‑course 5‑FU‑based chemoradiation or short‑course RT, depending on institutional protocol).  
   – Rationale: T3N2 upper rectal cancer requires down‑staging to facilitate sphincter‑preserving resection and to reduce local recurrence risk. Timing can be concurrent with chemotherapy (total‑neoadjuvant therapy) or sequential after systemic therapy.

C. Restaging work‑up (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT, and assessment of future liver remnant volume).  
   – Rationale: Determine response of hepatic lesions, reassess vascular involvement, calculate FLR. If FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan hypertrophy.

   – Rationale: Definitive control of the primary tumor is required for long‑term disease‑free survival.

   – Initiate 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents not indicated).

   – Repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) and thoraco‑abdominal imaging.  
   – Re‑evaluate lesion size, vascular involvement, and FLR adequacy.

   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and detect occult disease.

  • No reported major vascular or biliary invasion; absence of such involvement is a prerequisite for resectability.  
  • Extra‑hepatic work‑up is reported as negative for peritoneal and nodal disease; however, chest imaging and bone assessment are missing, and these are required to confirm true absence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
  • Adequate future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be confirmed because FLR ratio data are missing; sufficient FLR is essential before proceeding to surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging – Obtain thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) and bone imaging to definitively exclude pulmonary or skeletal metastases; repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast if needed.  
B. Systemic induction therapy – Initiate 3–4 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS‑wild‑type status, aiming to:  
   – Assess biologic response (CEA trend, radiologic shrinkage).  
   – Potentially eradicate the micronodule in segment V.

   – Perform a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of segment II and a wedge resection of the lesion in segment V (or combined non‑anatomical resections).  
   – Aim for R0 margins (> 1 cm when feasible).  
E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Resume systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively (e.g., additional 4–6 cycles) and consider maintenance anti‑EGFR therapy based on postoperative pathology and CEA trend.

Case_Content:
Woman, 71 years old, left colon cancer operated 5 years ago. Liver MRI: liver lesion segment V, 2.8 cm. CEA 90 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, favorable context, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable.  
• Rationale: The liver lesion is solitary, 2.8 cm, located in peripheral segment V, which is amenable to an anatomic segmentectomy with preservation of sufficient future liver remnant. No imaging evidence of major vascular or biliary invasion is provided, and the patient is described as being in good general condition. However, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed until extra‑hepatic disease is excluded and FLR volumetry is performed.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging  
   – Obtain a thoraco‑abdominal contrast‑enhanced CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases.  
   – Perform liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate FLR ratio and ensure ≥20‑30 % FLR in a non‑cirrhotic liver.

   – Initiate 2–3 months of standard doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status.

   – Repeat liver MRI and staging CT to confirm persistent solitary disease, absence of new lesions, and unchanged resectability criteria.  

D. Surgical resection  
   – Proceed with a laparoscopic or open segment V anatomical resection (segmentectomy) with intra‑operative ultrasound to verify margins and detect occult lesions.  
   – Aim for R0 resection with ≥1 cm margin when feasible.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy to complete a total of 6‑12 months of chemotherapy, tailored to response and tolerance.  
   – Monitor CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment V (2.8 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, history of rectal resection (T3N1) 2 years ago. Liver MRI: two liver metastases, segments II and VIII, 2.5 and 3 cm. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 240 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, technically accessible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Two metachronous liver metastases, each ≤3 cm, located in segments II and VIII – criteria compatible with curative resection.  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease (thoracic CT negative, peritoneal, bone and brain disease absent).  
  • Bilobar distribution but lesions are solitary in each lobe, allowing a parenchymal‑sparing approach (segmental resection or wedge).  
  • Missing data that could downgrade resectability: vascular or biliary involvement of the lesions, future liver remnant (FLR) volume, liver function tests, and performance status. Until FLR adequacy and absence of major vascular invasion are confirmed, the case remains “potentially” rather than definitively resectable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Baseline reassessment  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced liver CT (or repeat MRI) with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR ratio; assess portal vein anatomy and any vascular contact.  
   – Review laboratory profile (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelets) and performance status (ECOG).  
B. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Initiate 6 cycles of a modern oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR therapy is contraindicated due to KRAS mutation; consider adding bevacizumab.  
   – Rationale: high pre‑operative CEA (240 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology; systemic therapy provides disease control, tests tumor biology, and may increase resectability.  
C. Restaging after induction  
   – Repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
   – Re‑evaluate lesion size, vascular involvement, and FLR volume.  
   – If disease remains limited to the two lesions and FLR ≥30 % (≥20 % in chemotherapy‑treated liver), proceed to surgery.  
D. Surgical intervention  
   – Perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy: anatomical segment II resection and segment VIII wedge/segmentectomy, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound.  
   – Aim for R0 margins (≥1 cm when feasible).  
   – No need for simultaneous extra‑hepatic resection as extra‑hepatic sites are negative.  
E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 additional cycles) based on pathology and postoperative CEA trend.  
   – Schedule serial CEA and imaging surveillance every 3–6 months.
Reference:

The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases located in segments II and VIII (2.5 and 3 cm), without evidence of pulmonary disease. • Perform high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (240 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.

• Given the elevated CEA level (240 ng/mL) and relatively early recurrence (2 years), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
