• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability is confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing wedge/segmental resections or ablation of segments II and VIII guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Synchronous liver metastases have responded markedly to 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab (≈60 % volumetric reduction, CEA fall from 880 → 180 ng/mL).  
  • The residual disease consists of 5 well‑defined lesions, a number that is not an absolute contraindication when bilobar disease can be cleared with anatomic/non‑anatomic resections and/or ablation.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease has been reported on imaging, which, if confirmed, would support a curative intent.  
  • Critical data required to confirm technical resectability (lesion size, exact segmental distribution, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures, future liver remnant (FLR) volumetry, hepatic arterial/portal anatomy) are missing; therefore the case cannot be declared outright resectable at this stage.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete restaging  
   - Obtain high‑resolution thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast; perform volumetric CT to calculate FLR.  
   - Rationale: Confirm absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease and determine whether the FLR will be sufficient after planned hepatic resection.  

B. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - If the primary lesion has not yet been resected, perform oncologic colectomy (laparoscopic or open) with adequate lymphadenectomy.  
   - Rationale: Primary tumor control is required before or concomitantly with definitive liver surgery; simultaneous resection can be considered if operative risk is acceptable and FLR is adequate.  

C. Pre‑operative liver optimization (if needed)  
   - If FLR is <30 % in a normal liver (or <40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS).  
   - Rationale: Augment FLR to reduce postoperative liver failure risk.  

D. Definitive hepatic treatment  
   - Plan curative‑intent liver surgery: anatomical or non‑anatomical resections of all visible lesions combined with intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided ablation for lesions that would otherwise require an excessively large resection.  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 clearance of all hepatic disease while preserving sufficient liver parenchyma.  

E. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Resume or modify systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or switch to CAPOX) for 3–6 months, guided by molecular profile and postoperative pathology.  
   - Rationale: Consolidate surgical cure and address microscopic residual disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab, the patient shows a major radiologic and biologic response (≈60% volumetric reduction; CEA from 880 to 180 ng/mL). MRI now demonstrates five well-defined residual liver lesions without reported extrahepatic disease. In this context of marked downsizing and clearer lesion delineation, a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant appears potentially achievable. This pattern is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Immediate high-quality restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to reassess precise segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships after tumor shrinkage.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical conversion strategy
• If imaging confirms feasibility, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of all five lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may be performed as a single-stage or staged hepatectomy.
• The goal is complete clearance of residual disease while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic chemotherapy after recovery to complete a total of approximately 6 months of treatment (including preoperative cycles).

E. Surveillance
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Eight bilobar liver metastases exceed the typical “≤4 lesions” rule for straightforward single‑stage resection, but bilobar disease can be cleared with two‑stage hepatectomy, associating liver partition and portal vein embolization (ALPPS), or extensive parenchymal‑sparing resections if lesions are small and not vascularly encasing major structures.  
  • Disease is radiologically stable after 4 months of FOLFIRI, indicating no progression, which is a prerequisite for conversion intent.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoracic CT, satisfying the “no extra‑hepatic metastases” criterion for hepatic cure.  
  • Missing critical data (lesion size, proximity to major vessels/ biliary ducts, future liver remnant (FLR) volume, hepatic functional reserve) preclude a definitive “resectable” label; therefore the case remains in the potentially resectable/ conversion‑eligible category pending further assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue systemic therapy (FOLFIRI ± biologic agent based on molecular profile) for an additional 2–3 months to maximize tumor response and potentially induce lesion shrinkage.  
   – Rationale: Ongoing chemotherapy is the standard conversion approach for borderline hepatic disease; stable disease suggests tolerance and opportunity for further down‑staging.  

B. Perform comprehensive hepatic restaging: high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT if MRI unavailable) and volumetric analysis to determine lesion dimensions, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR. Include liver function assessment (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh, bilirubin, albumin) and performance status evaluation.  
   – Rationale: Precise anatomic and functional data are required to decide between single‑stage, two‑stage, or ALPPS approaches and to ensure postoperative liver safety.  

C. Multidisciplinary decision based on restaging results:  
   – If lesions are ≤3 cm, no major vascular encasement, and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in compromised liver), proceed with parenchymal‑sparing, simultaneous resection of all resectable lesions (single‑stage).  
   – If FLR is insufficient or lesions remain extensive, plan a staged strategy: (i) portal vein embolization or ligation of the future liver‑donor side, (ii) interval chemotherapy, (iii) second‑stage hepatectomy once FLR hypertrophies.  
   – Rationale: Tailors surgical aggressiveness to hepatic reserve while aiming for R0 resection.  

D. Post‑resection adjuvant systemic therapy (continue or switch regimen based on response and molecular markers) and regular surveillance (CEA, imaging every 3–4 months).  
   – Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence and monitors for new extra‑hepatic disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases and, after 4 months of FOLFIRI, shows radiological stability with persistently elevated CEA (420 ng/mL). The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and absence of meaningful tumor downsizing make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Continuation and adaptation of systemic therapy
• Given the absence of radiologic response and stable high CEA, modification of the systemic regimen should be considered according to MDT discussion.
• The objective remains to achieve tumor downsizing sufficient to allow potential secondary resectability.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to detect any delayed response or change in lesion distribution.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant reduction in lesion size and number occurs, enabling parenchymal-sparing resections or multiples ablations or staged hepatectomy with adequate future liver remnant.

D. Alternative local strategies
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (candidate for conversion to resection).  
- Rationale:  
  • Initial burden of ten liver metastases has been reduced by systemic therapy to seven residual lesions with a 40 % size decrease and radiologic signs of necrosis (hypo‑intense on hepatobiliary MRI), suggesting favorable tumor biology.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease on imaging, which, if absent, would allow a curative intent approach.  
  • Primary rectal tumor is not obstructed, perforated, or bleeding, indicating no immediate need for emergent resection.  
  • However, critical data required to confirm technical resectability are missing (exact lesion size, hepatic segments involved, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures, and future liver remnant (FLR) volume). Consequently, definitive resectability cannot be declared; the case remains in the “potentially resectable” category pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI ± biologic agent) for 2–3 additional cycles to maximize tumor shrinkage and assess CEA trend.  
   – Rationale: Consolidation of response may convert borderline lesions to resectable and allow better selection of patients who will benefit from surgery.  

B. Restaging work‑up after the additional cycles:  
   – Multiphasic liver MRI with volumetry to define residual lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR.  
   – Contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Repeat CEA measurement.  
   – Rationale: Precise anatomic mapping and exclusion of extra‑hepatic disease are mandatory before committing to hepatic resection.  

C. Multidisciplinary re‑evaluation of resectability:  
   – If imaging confirms that all residual liver disease can be removed with an adequate FLR (≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and no extra‑hepatic disease, plan curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   – Rationale: Ensures oncologic clearance while preserving postoperative liver function.  

D. Surgical sequencing (depending on primary tumor status):  
   1. If the rectal primary has not been resected and is amenable to neoadjuvant chemoradiation, deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy now, followed by delayed primary resection (low anterior resection) after hepatic surgery recovery.  
   2. If the primary is already resected or deemed low risk, proceed with a “liver‑first” approach: anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (potentially staged or combined with portal vein embolization if FLR insufficient).  
   – Rationale: Liver‑first strategy is preferred when hepatic disease is the dominant burden and systemic disease is controlled; it also avoids delay of potentially curative liver surgery.  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy:  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (or switch to maintenance) after recovery, tailored to molecular profile once available.  
   – Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence in the setting of high baseline CEA and multiple initial lesions.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Unresectable at this time  
- Rationale:  
  • Disease progression on first‑line FOLFOX (both hepatic lesions increased to 5.2 cm) indicates chemoresistance, a key adverse factor for surgical candidacy.  
  • Primary right‑colon tumor status unknown; lack of documented resection or control precludes a curative intent liver operation.  
  • No assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) or vascular/biliary involvement; without this data a safe R0 resection cannot be guaranteed.  
  • Although extra‑hepatic disease is not evident on current thoraco‑abdominal CT, the high CEA (950 ng/mL) and progression raise concern for occult disease.  
  • Current MDT conclusion (“no surgical window”) aligns with unresectable classification under contemporary hepatobiliary oncology criteria.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to delineate lesion morphology, vascular contact, and to calculate FLR.  
   - Perform high‑resolution chest MRI (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult pulmonary or brain metastases.  
   - Endoscopic evaluation of the primary tumor with biopsy to determine resectability and need for symptom control (obstruction, bleeding).  

B. Optimization of systemic therapy  
   - Switch to second‑line chemotherapy (FOLFIRI) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS mutation precluding anti‑EGFR agents.  
   - Consider enrollment in a clinical trial (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion, immunotherapy combinations) if available.  

C. Re‑assessment after 2–3 cycles of second‑line therapy  
   - Repeat imaging (MRI liver, CT chest/abdomen) to evaluate tumor response (stable disease or partial response).  
   - Re‑measure CEA; a declining trend would support continued medical therapy.  

D. Conditional surgical or ablative intervention  
   - If imaging shows disease control (no progression) and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury), plan for curative‑intent hepatic resection (right hepatectomy or extended right hepatectomy) combined with primary colon resection.  
   - If FLR insufficient, consider portal vein embolization to hypertrophy the remnant before resection.  
   - For lesions ≤3 cm after down‑staging, percutaneous ablation (RFA/MWA) may be an alternative or adjunct.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient shows progression of liver disease under FOLFOX with enlargement of two lesions in segments VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) and markedly elevated CEA (950 ng/mL). This radiologic progression under systemic therapy indicates biologically aggressive disease and makes a complete R0 resection with adequate oncologic control not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given progression on FOLFOX, a change of systemic regimen is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (conversion‑eligible).  
- Rationale:  
  • Seven hepatic lesions with radiologic complete response of four and shrinkage of the remaining three after 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab, indicating good chemosensitivity.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone disease assumed absent).  
  • Normalized CEA supports systemic disease control.  
  • Definitive resectability cannot be confirmed because critical data are missing (size of residual lesions, exact hepatic segments involved, relationship to major vessels/biliary structures, future liver remnant volume, and status of the primary colon tumor). These factors are required to determine whether an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy can achieve negative margins with adequate liver reserve.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT with 3‑D reconstruction) to delineate residual lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
   - Consider PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (including brain, if clinically indicated).  

B. Assessment and management of the primary tumor  
   - Verify whether the left‑sided colon primary has been resected; if not, schedule curative colectomy (laparoscopic or open) before or concurrently with liver surgery, depending on operative risk and tumor location.  

C. Multidisciplinary decision on hepatic surgery  
   - If imaging confirms that the remaining lesions are ≤3 cm, confined to ≤2‑3 segments, and away from major inflow/outflow structures, plan a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (segmentectomy/partial resection) or combined anatomic resection with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance.  
   - Ensure FLR ≥30 % in a normal liver (or ≥40 % if prior chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected). If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) as bridge to definitive resection.  

D. Post‑operative/adjuvant management  
   - Resume systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of anti‑EGFR‑containing regimen or switch to maintenance) after wound healing, guided by pathology (margin status, tumor regression grade, molecular profile).  
   - Implement surveillance with serial CEA and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab, four lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions have significantly decreased in size, with normalization of CEA. Despite this excellent response, the initial tumor burden and the phenomenon of “disappearing metastases” mean that viable microscopic disease may persist at the original sites. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but requires meticulous mapping of all initial metastatic locations before surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and systematically compare with pre-treatment imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy addressing initial disease map
• Plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided surgical approach that includes resection or ablation of all initial metastatic locations, not only residual visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to identify occult residual disease.
• Depending on lesion distribution, this may require a staged approach.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete surgical clearance of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Liver: three residual lesions each <2 cm, no capsular infiltration, no infiltrative pattern reported; size and number fall within conventional criteria for hepatic resection.  
  • Systemic therapy produced a major radiologic response and a marked CEA decline, indicating favorable tumor biology (RAS wild‑type).  
  • Absence of documented vascular or biliary invasion suggests that an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection could achieve negative margins.  
  • Resectability cannot be confirmed without data on hepatic segmental distribution, future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and the presence/absence of extra‑hepatic disease; therefore the case remains “potentially” rather than definitively resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete staging  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and high‑resolution pelvic MRI to:  
     • Exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes, bone, brain).  
     • Define the exact hepatic segmental location of each lesion and assess vascular/biliary relationships.  
     • Evaluate the rectal primary for depth of invasion, mesorectal fascia involvement, and need for neoadjuvant chemoradiation.  
   – Calculate FLR using volumetric CT or MRI; consider portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR <30 % in a normal liver.  

B. Management of the rectal primary  
   – If the rectal tumor is locally advanced (cT3‑4 or threatened mesorectal fascia), deliver standard long‑course chemoradiotherapy (45‑50 Gy with concurrent 5‑FU/Capecitabine).  
   – Re‑stage 6‑8 weeks after chemoradiation; proceed to total mesorectal excision (TME) if resectable and no distant progression.  

C. Continuation of systemic therapy  
   – Maintain or complete a total of 6‑8 cycles of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) after liver assessment, aiming to consolidate response and treat micrometastatic disease.  

D. Surgical resection of liver metastases  
   – Once extra‑hepatic disease is excluded, FLR is adequate, and the rectal primary is either already resected or scheduled, perform hepatic resection:  
     • Preferred approach: parenchymal‑sparing non‑anatomic or segmental resections of the three lesions, aiming for R0 margins.  
     – Timing:  
        • If rectal chemoradiation is required, a “liver‑first” (hepatectomy before TME) or staged approach (hepatectomy → recovery → TME) is reasonable, given the small hepatic burden and good response.  
        • If the rectal tumor is low‑risk and can be resected without neoadjuvant therapy, a simultaneous colorectal‑liver operation may be considered in a high‑volume center.  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑6 months) after recovery from surgery, tailored to pathology (margin status, nodal involvement).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal sites assumed absent).  
  • Bilobar liver metastases are present, but the number, size, segmental distribution, and relationship to major vessels are unknown; these factors are critical to determine whether an R0 resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) is feasible.  
  • The primary transverse colon tumor has not been reported as resected; resectability of the primary must be incorporated into the overall plan.  
  • Limited progression on FOLFOX (two new lesions) indicates that disease control is suboptimal, raising concern for systemic spread, but does not yet preclude a surgical attempt if a favorable response can be achieved with an alternative regimen.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, and perform volumetric CT to calculate FLR.  
   - Complete molecular profiling of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H, HER2) and assess tumor grade.  
   - Re‑evaluate the primary colon lesion (endoscopic assessment, CT colonography) to determine resectability and need for symptom control.  

B. Systemic therapy optimization  
   - Switch to a more intensive conversion regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) or add targeted agents based on molecular results, aiming for maximal tumor shrinkage and control of the new hepatic lesions.  
   - Monitor CEA trend and repeat imaging after 2–3 cycles to assess response.  

C. Surgical planning (contingent on response)  
   - If imaging shows reduction of hepatic disease to a resectable burden (≤4 lesions, ≤5 cm each, no major vascular invasion, and FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), proceed with a combined or staged approach:  
        • First, resect or control the primary transverse colon tumor (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
        • Second, perform liver resection—either a single‑stage parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy if feasible, or a two‑stage/ALPPS strategy if FLR is insufficient.  
   - Ensure intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and vascular anatomy.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume systemic therapy post‑operatively (e.g., continuation of bevacizumab or switch to maintenance capecitabine/oxaliplatin) for at least 6 months, tailored to molecular profile.  
   - Schedule CEA monitoring and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then semi‑annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases with the appearance of two new lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression under systemic therapy. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and ongoing progression make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The appearance of new lesions under FOLFOX indicates resistance to the current regimen.
• A change of systemic protocol is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± targeted therapy depending on molecular profile).
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
  • Ten hepatic lesions were present initially; after systemic therapy three have disappeared and six are stable, leaving a single progressing lesion (5 cm in segment VII).  
  • A solitary lesion of this size can be surgically removed (segmentectomy or extended hepatectomy) provided adequate future liver remnant (FLR) and absence of major vascular or biliary invasion.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease has been documented, but thoracic imaging and comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging are lacking, preventing a definitive “resectable” label.  
  • FLR assessment, vascular involvement, and extra‑hepatic status are required to move from “potentially resectable” to “resectable.”  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete restaging – obtain thoraco‑abdominal CT (including chest), liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, and PET‑CT; measure serum CEA; calculate FLR volume (CT volumetry or MRI) and evaluate portal venous anatomy. Rationale: defines true disease burden, confirms absence of extra‑hepatic metastases, and determines whether the liver remnant will be sufficient after resection.  

B. Continue systemic chemotherapy – maintain or intensify current regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) with addition of biologic agent appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease (anti‑VEGF). Rationale: aims to achieve further tumor shrinkage of the progressing segment VII lesion and to treat any occult microscopic disease.  

C. Local control of the progressing hepatic lesion – if after restaging the lesion remains solitary and resectable, proceed with either:  
   • Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right liver (or appropriate sector) to augment FLR, followed by anatomical resection of segment VII (or right hepatectomy if required); or  
   • Image‑guided ablative therapy (microwave or radiofrequency) if FLR is insufficient or vascular involvement precludes safe resection.  
   Rationale: addresses the only site of progression while preserving hepatic function.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor – if the primary has not yet been resected, schedule curative colectomy (preferably after hepatic control, but simultaneous resection can be considered if patient fitness permits and operative time is acceptable). Rationale: eliminates the source of further metastatic seeding and completes oncologic treatment of the primary.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (requires further evaluation).  
• Justification:  
  – Initial disease was bilobar, indicating that a curative‑intent liver resection would be technically demanding and would depend on future liver remnant (FLR) adequacy, which is not reported.  
  – Post‑chemotherapy imaging shows a radiologic complete response, but occult viable tumor can persist despite disappearance on CT; therefore surgical exploration or high‑resolution imaging is needed before declaring resectability.  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on current scans, which is favorable.  
  – Absence of data on vascular involvement, lesion size, number, and FLR prevents a definitive “resectable” label.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and high‑resolution imaging  
   – Obtain liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences (and gadoxetate if available) and a PET‑CT to detect residual hepatic or occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Perform pelvic MRI and/or endoscopic evaluation to define the status of the rectal primary (size, depth, mesorectal nodes).  
   – Rationale: Accurate mapping will confirm true complete response, assess FLR, and guide surgical planning.  

B. Assessment of the rectal primary  
   – If the primary tumor has not been resected, initiate standard neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced rectal cancer, followed by total mesorectal excision (TME).  
   – Rationale: Control of the primary lesion is essential before any definitive liver‑directed surgery and improves oncologic outcomes.  

C. Surgical exploration of the liver (or ablative approach)  
   – If imaging suggests residual disease or if the FLR is adequate, proceed with intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided liver resection or, alternatively, parenchymal‑sparing resections/ablation of any detectable lesions.  
   – If no viable disease is identified, consider a “watch‑and‑wait” policy with close surveillance rather than prophylactic resection.  
   – Rationale: Surgical clearance offers the only chance for cure when viable disease persists; otherwise, unnecessary hepatectomy carries morbidity without benefit.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy and surveillance  
   – Depending on pathology (if resection performed) and molecular profile, continue or de‑escalate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., maintenance FOLFOX or capecitabine).  
   – Implement a surveillance schedule: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   – Rationale: High risk of recurrence after initial metastatic disease warrants continued systemic control and early detection of relapse.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline) but not currently resectable.  
- Rationale: Three hepatic lesions each >5 cm after 8 cycles of chemotherapy indicate bulky disease; MDT already judged “partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.” Critical determinants for resectability (segmental distribution, vascular or biliary invasion, future liver remnant volume, and presence of extra‑hepatic disease) are not documented, preventing a definitive resectable designation. The lesions remain technically resectable only if down‑staged to ≤5 cm, limited to ≤4 lesions, with adequate FLR and no major vascular involvement.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue systemic conversion therapy  
   • Maintain or intensify current chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOX/FOLFIRI) and add biologic agent based on molecular profile (anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type, anti‑VEGF otherwise).  
   • Goal: achieve further tumor shrinkage to meet resectability criteria.  

B. Comprehensive restaging imaging  
   • Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, triphasic abdominal CT, and thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic CT (or PET‑CT) to define lesion number, segmental location, vascular/biliary involvement, and to detect occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  

C. Re‑assessment of resectability after imaging  
   • If lesions reduce to ≤5 cm, involve ≤4 segments, and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % in steatotic liver), proceed to surgical planning.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to augment remnant.  

D. Surgical phase (when criteria met)  
   • Simultaneous or staged resection of the primary right‑colon tumor (if not already removed) together with curative‑intent liver resection (anatomical or non‑anatomical) aiming for R0 margins.  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and assess vascular anatomy.  

E. If down‑staging fails or extra‑hepatic disease is identified  
   • Evaluate local ablative options (radiofrequency or microwave ablation) for lesions unsuitable for resection.  
   • Consider continuation of systemic therapy with best‑supportive care, enrolling in clinical trials if appropriate.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable.  
• Rationale:  
  – Two isolated hepatic lesions (2.1 cm in segment II, 3.4 cm in segment III) with no vascular or biliary invasion.  
  – No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease.  
  – Prior right hepatectomy leaves left liver (segments II‑IV) as remnant; removal of segments II‑III would leave only segment IV (and caudate) as future liver remnant (FLR).  
  – Adequacy of FLR has not been quantified; without volumetric data the FLR is likely borderline (<20 % of total liver volume), making the case “potentially” rather than outright resectable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and complete staging  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and a triphasic liver CT to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease and to delineate arterial, portal and hepatic venous anatomy.  
   – Perform CT volumetry (or MRI volumetry) to calculate the FLR after a hypothetical left‑lateral (II‑III) resection.  

B. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
   – Initiate a KRAS‑mutated regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially down‑size the lesions.  

C. FLR optimization (if FLR insufficient)  
   – If volumetry shows FLR <20‑30 % (depending on liver quality), proceed with portal vein embolization of the portal branches feeding segments II‑III (segmental PVE) or consider a staged approach (e.g., ALPPS‑type hypertrophy) to induce hypertrophy of segment IV.  

D. Definitive local treatment  
   – If post‑PVE FLR becomes adequate, perform a left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) with intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 margins.  
   – If FLR remains inadequate or patient is unfit for major resection, treat the lesions with percutaneous ablative modalities (RFA/MWA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy as an alternative parenchymal‑sparing strategy.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume systemic therapy (adjuvant or continuation) based on pathological response and multidisciplinary discussion.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm) occurring in the left lateral section after a prior right hepatectomy, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesions are peripherally located but arise in the only remaining functional liver. Resection is technically feasible but must strictly preserve adequate parenchyma and inflow/outflow. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable with a strict parenchymal-sparing strategy, pending volumetric confirmation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative volumetric and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and ensure preservation of sufficient functional parenchyma.
• Assess portal inflow and venous outflow carefully given prior right hepatectomy.

B. Peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (220 ng/mL) and early recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the 2 lesions of segments II and III aiming for R0 margins.
• Avoid any formal left hepatectomy or extended resection.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of left R0 hepatectomy for liver metastases three years ago. CEA 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VIII (3.8 cm) in contact with the IVC. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep solitary recurrence, technical assessment of resection required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (not outright resectable nor unresectable).  
• Rationale:  
  – Single metachronous liver lesion, 3.8 cm, confined to segment VIII, meets size and number criteria for hepatic resection.  
  – Prior left hepatectomy reduces future liver remnant; FLR volume is unknown, therefore adequacy cannot be confirmed.  
  – Lesion contacts the inferior vena cava, raising concern for vascular invasion; resection may require IVC control or reconstruction, which is technically feasible in experienced centers but must be evaluated.  
  – No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but imaging of chest/abdomen is missing; absence of extra‑hepatic metastases is required for curative intent.  
  – High CEA (180 ng/mL) suggests active disease; response to systemic therapy would help confirm biologic aggressiveness.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with volumetry; assess IVC involvement depth, hepatic arterial/portal anatomy, and calculate FLR ratio.  
   – Obtain full laboratory panel (LFTs, bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance) and assess performance status/comorbidities.  
   Rationale: Determines true resectability, FLR adequacy, and rules out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status.  
   Rationale: Treats potential micrometastatic disease, may down‑size the IVC‑contacting lesion, and provides a biologic test of disease control (CEA trend, radiologic response).  

C. Re‑assessment and operative planning  
   – Repeat imaging after chemotherapy; if lesion remains resectable and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if underlying liver disease), proceed to hepatic resection.  
   – If FLR insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) before definitive resection.  
   – Plan for segment VIII resection with possible IVC tangential resection or patch repair; involve vascular surgery for reconstruction if needed.  
   Rationale: Ensures safe hepatic reserve and addresses vascular involvement while aiming for R0 margins.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   – Pathologic assessment of margins and response; if R0 achieved, resume adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months systemic therapy.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance per standard guidelines.  
   Rationale: Consolidates oncologic control and detects early recurrence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver recurrence in segment VIII (3.8 cm) occurring after a prior left R0 hepatectomy. The lesion is deep and in contact with the IVC, in the only remaining right liver. Although solitary, the location adjacent to the IVC and the reduced liver reserve make resection technically demanding. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable, pending detailed vascular and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform expert liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to precisely evaluate the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and right hepatic vein.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and assess inflow/outflow preservation.
• Evaluate whether R0 resection can be achieved without caval reconstruction.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (180 ng/mL) and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status) may be considered to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing mandatory)
• If resectability is confirmed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, history of segmental VI-VII resection. Liver MRI: new lesion segment III (2.4 cm) and micronodule segment II. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous contralateral recurrence, possible minimally invasive approach depending on remnant volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Metachronous liver disease with only two lesions (segment III 2.4 cm and a micronodule in segment II) that are small and located in the left lateral sector, a region amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resection.  
  • Prior resection was limited to segments VI‑VII, leaving the left liver largely untouched; therefore a reasonable future liver remnant (FLR) is likely, pending volumetric confirmation.  
  • No reported major vascular or biliary invasion, and no documented extra‑hepatic disease, which are key criteria for resectability.  
  • However, definitive assessment requires confirmation of FLR volume, vascular anatomy, and exclusion of extra‑hepatic metastases; in their absence the case remains “potentially” rather than definitively resectable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to evaluate for occult extra‑hepatic disease, vascular involvement, and to obtain accurate FLR volumetry.  
   - Measure serum CEA and obtain colonoscopic evaluation of the primary tumor (if not already resected) to define residual disease.  

B. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant/ peri‑operative)  
   - If FLR is adequate and no extra‑hepatic disease is found, initiate a short course (2–3 months) of oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) ± anti‑EGFR or anti‑VEGF biologic according to RAS status (to be determined).  
   - Goal: eradicate micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially down‑size the micronodule.  

C. Surgical resection  
   - Proceed with minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) left lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) using a parenchymal‑sparing technique; consider intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate the micronodule and to confirm absence of additional lesions.  
   - If FLR is borderline (<30 % in a chemotherapy‑injured liver), consider portal vein embolization of the right portal branches or a two‑stage approach before definitive resection.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   - Pathology review to determine margin status and tumor regression grade.  
   - Resume/adapt systemic therapy based on pathology and molecular profile (e.g., adjuvant FOLFOX for high‑risk features).  
   - Implement a structured surveillance program (CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging every 6 months for the first 2 years).

• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both approaches.

• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

MDT Discussion: Isolated complex recurrence of the hepatic dome, technical assessment required.

- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)

  • Single hepatic lesion, 3.1 cm, meeting size criteria for curative resection.

  • Prior left hepatectomy leaves a right‑lobe remnant; removal of a segment VIII lesion is unlikely to compromise overall liver volume, but the exact future liver remnant (FLR) ratio has not been quantified.  
  • Contact with the middle hepatic vein introduces technical complexity (possible venous resection/reconstruction) but does not automatically preclude resection.  
  • Elevated CEA (200 ng/mL) suggests active disease; systemic disease control should be confirmed before definitive surgery.

A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic metastases and to delineate vascular involvement.  
   – Obtain laboratory panel (LFTs, bilirubin, INR, albumin) and calculate volumetric FLR using CT‑based software.

C. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
   – Initiate an effective chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR agent based on molecular profile) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology, potentially down‑size the lesion, and treat occult micrometastatic disease.  

D. Re‑assessment after systemic therapy  
   – Repeat imaging to evaluate response of the segment VIII lesion and to verify that no new extra‑hepatic disease has emerged.  
   – Re‑calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % (or <40 % in compromised liver), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the remnant before surgery.  

E. Surgical intervention (if still resectable)  
   – Perform a parenchyma‑sparing resection (segmentectomy of VIII) with careful dissection of the middle hepatic vein; if venous invasion is confirmed, resect the involved segment of the vein with primary repair or graft reconstruction.  
   – Aim for R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries.  

F. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume/adapt systemic therapy based on pathological response and molecular findings.  
   – Monitor CEA and imaging surveillance per standard protocols.

Case_Content:

MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:

- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale: Single 3.9 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT, and prior resection was limited to segments IV‑V, leaving sufficient hepatic parenchyma in theory. KRAS mutation does not preclude surgery. Definitive resectability hinges on (a) future liver remnant (FLR) volume and function, (b) absence of major vascular or biliary invasion, and (c) adequate patient performance status – data not yet provided.

A. Restaging and baseline work‑up  
   • Obtain serum CEA, full liver panel, and assess performance status.  
   • Review colonoscopy or imaging to confirm that the primary colorectal lesion has been resected with clear margins; if not, plan for primary tumor management.  
   • Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR ratio and evaluate for any occult vascular contact of the segment VII lesion.

   • Initiate standard first‑line chemotherapy for KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 2–3 months to address micrometastatic disease and potentially downsize the lesion, unless rapid surgery is deemed safe based on FLR.

   • If FLR ≥ 30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver (or ≥ 40 % if borderline function) and no major vascular involvement, proceed with an anatomic segmentectomy of VII (or wedge resection with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance).

D. Post‑operative/adjuvant phase  
   • Resume/continue systemic chemotherapy for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative therapy.  
   • Consider enrollment in a clinical trial or use of targeted agents appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease.  
   • Implement surveillance protocol: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years.

Case_Content:
Man, 72 years old, right hepatectomy 4 years ago. Current liver MRI: multiple nodules segment III, 1-2 cm. CEA 550 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Multifocal recurrence, assessment of resectability and local alternatives.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable.  
• Rationale: The only reported hepatic disease is a cluster of 1‑2 cm nodules confined to segment III, a peripheral left‑lateral sector that can be removed with a limited segmentectomy or wedge resection while preserving the remaining left liver (segments II and IV). Prior right hepatectomy leaves sufficient parenchyma in theory, but the exact future liver remnant (FLR) volume, liver function, and presence of vascular or biliary involvement are unknown. Absence of documented extra‑hepatic disease on imaging also supports potential resectability, but definitive assessment requires completion of staging studies and volumetry.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or osseous metastases.  
   – Perform liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets) and calculate Child‑Pugh/ALBI scores.  
   – Conduct volumetric CT or MRI to determine FLR percentage; consider portal‑vein embolization (PVE) if FLR < 30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver.  
   – Rationale: Accurate assessment of extra‑hepatic disease, hepatic reserve, and FLR is mandatory before committing to surgery.

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (if no contraindication)  
   – Initiate a standard oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS‑wild‑type status.  
   – Duration: 2–3 months, with imaging reassessment thereafter.  
   – Rationale: Provides a test of tumor biology, may eradicate occult micrometastases, and can modestly shrink lesions to facilitate a margin‑negative resection.

C. Surgical resection (contingent on step A/B results)  
   – Perform an anatomic segment III resection or non‑anatomic wedge excision with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance to ensure negative margins (R0) and to assess for additional occult lesions.  
   – Preserve segments II and IV to maintain adequate FLR; consider intra‑operative portal flow assessment.  
   – Rationale: Limited resection offers curative intent while minimizing loss of functional liver parenchyma in a patient with prior right hepatectomy.

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance  
   – Resume or continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6‑month total duration) after recovery from surgery, tailored to postoperative pathology and response.  
   – Schedule serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   – Rationale: Consolidates disease control and enables early detection of recurrence.
