Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (neither clearly resectable nor unresectable).  
- Rationale:  
  • Three liver metastases each ≤4 cm are within the size and number limits that can be cleared with an R0 hepatectomy, provided adequate future liver remnant (FLR) and no major vascular or biliary invasion.  
  • Bilateral pulmonary nodules represent limited extra‑hepatic disease; when few and amenable to metastasectomy, they do not automatically preclude curative intent.  
  • Absence of data on hepatic segmental distribution, vascular contact, FLR ratio, and response to systemic therapy prevents a definitive “resectable” label.  
  • Presence of T4 primary tumor and N2 nodal stage indicates aggressive biology, reinforcing the need for neoadjuvant systemic therapy before committing to surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6‑12 weeks of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab; anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective with KRAS mutation).  
   – Rationale: Down‑size liver and lung lesions, treat micrometastatic disease, and assess tumor biology.  

B. Restaging work‑up after chemotherapy:  
   – Multiphasic liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define segmental involvement, vascular/biliary proximity, and calculate FLR.  
   – FDG‑PET/CT to confirm pulmonary nodules are metastatic and to exclude occult extra‑hepatic sites.  
   – Repeat high‑resolution chest CT to measure pulmonary nodule size and relationship to vessels/bronchi.  
   – Laboratory assessment (liver function, CEA trend, performance status).  
   – Rationale: Determine resectability, guide surgical sequencing, and identify patients who may become unresectable.  

C. Surgical sequencing (chosen after restaging confirms resectability):  
   1. If the primary colon lesion is still in situ and symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding), perform colectomy first; otherwise consider a “liver‑first” approach because hepatic disease is the dominant prognostic factor.  
   2. Perform curative‑intent liver resection aiming for R0 margins and preserving ≥20‑30 % FLR (or use portal vein embolization if FLR insufficient).  
   3. After hepatic recovery (4‑6 weeks), reassess pulmonary nodules; if still resectable, proceed with staged thoracic metastasectomy (video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery or open, depending on size/location).  
   – Rationale: Allows maximal clearance of intra‑hepatic disease while minimizing peri‑operative risk; staged pulmonary resection reduces cumulative morbidity.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy:  
   – Resume or continue systemic therapy (e.g., maintenance bevacizumab or fluoropyrimidine) after completion of all surgical procedures, guided by postoperative CEA and imaging.  
   – Rationale: Consolidate response and address any residual microscopic disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases (2–4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules in the setting of a left T4N2 colon cancer, without other reported sites. The presence of limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lungs) does not preclude a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be cleared. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically resectable. This situation is considered potentially resectable in a multimodal, sequential curative strategy, provided both hepatic and pulmonary disease are amenable to complete treatment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.
• Given the high CEA level (620 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given synchronous extrahepatic disease and high CEA (620 ng/mL), initiate systemic douhlet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab)
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at all sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Sequential surgical strategy after response
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon primary) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

	2.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
	3.	Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• The sequence (liver-first vs lung-first) depends on response and technical considerations.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale: The patient has four liver metastases ≤3.8 cm, which can be technically resected provided an adequate future liver remnant and no major vascular invasion. However, the presence of nodular peritoneal disease represents extra‑hepatic spread that precludes an upfront curative hepatectomy. Current guidelines consider liver‑only disease resectable, but concurrent peritoneal metastases require either confirmation of limited peritoneal burden (low PCI) or down‑staging before a combined curative approach. Therefore, resectability cannot be confirmed at this stage; the case is deemed potentially resectable pending further systemic response and detailed peritoneal assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to achieve tumor shrinkage in both liver and peritoneum and to assess tumor biology.  
B. Restaging and detailed imaging  
   - Perform liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, PET‑CT, and diagnostic laparoscopy with PCI scoring to define hepatic segmental involvement, vascular contact, FLR calculation, and peritoneal disease extent.  
C. Multimodal curative surgery (if criteria met)  
   - If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows ≤3 liver lesions amenable to R0 resection with FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy) and PCI ≤ 10 with resectable peritoneal nodules, proceed to combined liver resection plus cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC). The sequence can be simultaneous (single‑stage) or staged (liver first, then CRS/HIPEC) based on intra‑operative assessment and patient fitness.  
D. Continuation of systemic therapy / palliation  
   - If disease remains extensive (e.g., high PCI, unresectable vascular involvement, insufficient FLR), continue systemic therapy, consider targeted/immune agents according to molecular profile, and focus on symptom control and best‑supportive care.
Reference:
Step 1 - The patient presents with four liver metastases (1.5–3.8 cm) associated with nodular peritoneal involvement on CT. The presence of peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. According to oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable from a hepatobiliary perspective in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (950 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.
• The goal is to evaluate tumor biology and potential response at both hepatic and peritoneal sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Current classification: Potentially resectable (neither clearly resectable nor unresectable).  
• Rationale:  
  – Synchronous mid‑rectal T3N1 primary with RAS‑wild‑type status; rectal primary is amenable to curative resection (TME) after appropriate neoadjuvant therapy.  
  – Five bilobar liver metastases: bilobar distribution does not preclude resection, but resectability depends on lesion size, segmental location, vascular/biliary involvement, and future liver remnant (FLR) adequacy, which are not provided.  
  – Single right‑lung metastasis: isolated pulmonary metastasis can be resected if technically feasible and disease‑free interval is acceptable; size and anatomic relationship to vessels/bronchi are unknown.  
  – Absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the lung lesion and no peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases reported.  
  – Therefore, with appropriate down‑staging systemic therapy and completion of missing anatomic data, a curative‑intent combined approach remains plausible.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (2–3 months)  
   – Regimen: FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX) plus anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS‑wild‑type status.  
   – Goal: tumor shrinkage of liver lesions, possible conversion of marginally resectable lesions, and assessment of tumor biology (CEA trend).  

B. Restaging work‑up (after neoadjuvant therapy)  
   – High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define number, size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR.  
   – PET‑CT to confirm metabolic response of hepatic and pulmonary lesions and to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Chest CT with thin slices to detail the right‑lung nodule (size, location, relation to vessels/bronchi).  
   – Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy to reassess rectal tumor; consider MRI pelvis for local staging.  

C. Multidisciplinary decision on surgical sequencing (based on restaging)  
   – If all sites become resectable and FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if liver steatosis/chemotherapy‑associated injury), proceed to curative surgery.  
   – Preferred sequence:  
     1. Rectal primary – total mesorectal excision (TME) after standard long‑course chemoradiation (if not already given) to achieve local control.  
     2. Liver resection – either single‑stage (if FLR adequate) or two‑stage/ALPPS (if insufficient FLR) to clear all hepatic lesions.  
     3. Pulmonary metastasectomy – right‑sided wedge resection or segmentectomy performed either simultaneously with liver surgery (if operative risk acceptable) or as a staged procedure within 4–6 weeks after hepatic resection.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Resume/continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months total exposure) post‑operatively, tailored to pathologic response and residual disease risk.  

E. Surveillance  
   – Serial CEA measurements every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not contraindicate a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. • Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.

• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.

• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.

-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement associated with extra-hepatic lymph nodes, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (requires further evaluation).  
- Rationale:  
  • Six hepatic lesions – number alone does not preclude resection if they can be cleared with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Presence of hepatic‑pedicle lymph node metastasis – extra‑hepatic disease, but limited nodal spread can be addressed surgically in selected patients.  
  • No reported major vascular or biliary invasion; however this information is missing and must be confirmed.  
  • KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA (780 ng/mL) suggest aggressive biology, favoring neoadjuvant systemic therapy before any operative attempt.  
  • Absence of documented distant organ metastases (lung, bone, brain) makes a curative approach feasible pending complete staging and FLR assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   – Aim: tumor down‑staging, assess biologic response, treat occult micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging work‑up after chemotherapy:  
   – High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast.  
   – Chest CT (to rule out pulmonary mets).  
   – FDG‑PET/CT (to characterize hepatic‑pedicle nodes and detect other occult sites).  
   – Volumetric CT to calculate FLR ratio.  

C. Multidisciplinary reassessment of resectability based on restaging data.  
   – If all hepatic lesions can be cleared with ≥ 30 % FLR (≥ 40 % in compromised liver) and nodal disease is limited and resectable, proceed to surgery.  

D. Surgical phase (if deemed resectable):  
   – Option 1 – Simultaneous resection of liver metastases and hepatic‑pedicle lymphadenectomy, provided operative risk is acceptable and FLR is adequate.  
   – Option 2 – Staged approach (e.g., portal vein embolization to augment FLR followed by hepatic resection, then nodal clearance) if FLR is marginal.  
   – Goal: R0 resection of all hepatic lesions and involved nodes while preserving sufficient liver function.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy post‑operatively (same regimen or tailored based on response) for at least 3–6 months.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions and other para-aortic enlarged lymph nodes

Case_Content:

MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Current classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
• Rationale: The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases, which can be resectable only if an R0 resection is achievable with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy). No data are provided on the number of lesions, their size, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, or FLR calculation, all of which are essential to determine technical resectability.  
• The presence of a solitary cerebellar metastasis makes the disease systemic; however, isolated brain metastasis can be treated definitively, after which hepatic and colorectal surgery may be pursued if the liver disease can be cleared. Consequently, the case is not outright unresectable but remains uncertain pending further information.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neurosurgical / radiosurgical management of the cerebellar lesion – immediate priority to prevent neurologic deterioration. Options include stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or microsurgical resection depending on lesion size, edema, and symptomatic status.  
B. Systemic chemotherapy with conversion intent – initiate a modern doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) after brain lesion control.    • If the primary colon tumor has not been removed and is symptomatic or at risk of complications, perform a right hemicolectomy (simultaneous with liver resection if operative risk acceptable, otherwise staged).  
   • Perform curative‑intent liver resection (single‑stage if all lesions can be cleared with adequate FLR, or two‑stage/ALPPS if bilobar disease requires staged approach). Aim for R0 margins.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the primary tumor
• Right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the mediastinal metastases
• Plan mediatinal lymphadenectomy in a staged manner.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T4N2 rectal tumor, six bilobar liver metastases, pulmonary micronodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1250 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable after conversion therapy.  
- Justification:  
  • Six bilobar liver metastases exceed the typical criteria for upfront resection (generally ≤4 lesions or unilobar disease).  
  • Presence of pulmonary micronodules represents limited extra‑hepatic disease; when few and stable, they do not preclude curative intent.  
  • RAS wild‑type status predicts good response to modern systemic regimens (e.g., anti‑EGFR or bevacizumab‑based).  
  • No documented vascular invasion or insufficient future liver remnant (FLR) data; therefore, resectability cannot be excluded pending further assessment.  
  • MDT already deemed “not resectable upfront,” supporting the need for down‑staging before surgical consideration.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (and concurrent rectal chemoradiation if indicated)  
   – Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + anti‑EGFR) for 8–12 weeks.  
   – Rationale: Aim for maximal tumor shrinkage in liver and lung, assess biological response, and control the locally advanced T4 rectal primary.  

B. Restaging after induction  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT, and FDG‑PET/CT.  
   – Rationale: Precisely quantify residual hepatic disease (size, segmental distribution, vascular contact), evaluate pulmonary nodules (number, size, metabolic activity), and calculate FLR.  

C. Decision point based on response  
   – If ≥70 % radiologic response in liver and pulmonary lesions become ≤5 mm or disappear, proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
   – If response insufficient, consider alternative systemic regimen or continue conversion therapy.  

D. Surgical sequence (when criteria met)  
   1. Primary rectal tumor: total mesorectal excision (TME) after completion of neoadjuvant chemoradiation, unless obstructive/bleeding symptoms mandate earlier resection.  
   2. Liver metastases:  
      – If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % after chemotherapy) and disease is unilobar after response, perform single‑stage anatomical resection.  
      – If FLR inadequate or disease remains bilobar, plan a two‑stage hepatectomy with portal vein embolization (PVE) after first stage to hypertrophy the remnant.  
   3. Pulmonary metastases: limited‑size nodules (≤5 mm) may be observed; larger or progressive lesions should be resected (wedge or segmentectomy) synchronously with liver surgery if feasible, or staged thereafter.  
   – Rationale: Sequencing ensures control of the primary, maximizes hepatic reserve, and addresses all resectable disease in a curative‑intent framework.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules in the context of a T4N2 rectal tumor and very high CEA (1250 ng/mL). The combination of extensive bilobar hepatic disease and extrahepatic pulmonary involvement reflects advanced systemic dissemination. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.
• Given the high CEA level (1250 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• Start systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare case of major response with significant reduction of both hepatic and pulmonary disease, allowing complete clearance of all sites.
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.

F. Pelvic management integration
• Plan rectal treatment (short-course radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy) according the MDT discussion if the primary tumor is symptomatic

G. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

H. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• If resection, analysis ofpathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (subject to further clarification).  
• Rationale:  
   – Liver disease is confined to three hepatic segments (IV, V, VIII) without documented major vascular or biliary invasion, suggesting that a curative‑intent hepatectomy could be technically feasible if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
   – The presence of a solitary right iliac bone metastasis represents limited extra‑hepatic disease; current oncologic guidelines allow hepatic resection in the setting of oligometastatic bone disease provided the bone lesion can be controlled (e.g., radiotherapy, surgical stabilization) and systemic disease is otherwise responsive.  
   – KRAS mutation does not preclude surgery but indicates the need for an appropriate systemic regimen.  
   – Definitive assessment of resectability is pending data on the number and size of liver lesions, relationship to major vessels/portal structures, FLR volume, and response to systemic therapy.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as first‑line therapy to treat both hepatic and bone disease and to assess tumor biology.  
   – Rationale: Systemic control is prioritized by the MDT; chemotherapy can downsize liver lesions, treat occult disease, and provide a test of disease responsiveness.  

B. Perform comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months of systemic therapy:  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase, thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic CT, and bone scan or PET‑CT to evaluate response of hepatic lesions, FLR adequacy, and bone lesion status.  
   – Rationale: Precise imaging is required to determine the number, size, and vascular proximity of liver metastases and to reassess extra‑hepatic burden.  

C. Address the right iliac bone metastasis with local therapy (palliative radiotherapy or surgical fixation) if symptomatic, at risk of fracture, or if it remains active after systemic therapy.  
   – Rationale: Controlling the bone lesion prevents skeletal complications and fulfills the “controlled extra‑hepatic disease” prerequisite for curative hepatic surgery.  

D. If restaging demonstrates: (i) limited hepatic disease amenable to resection with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a steatotic liver), (ii) no new extra‑hepatic sites, and (iii) adequate performance status, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy of segments IV, V, VIII).  
   – Rationale: Achieving R0 resection of all hepatic metastases offers the best chance for long‑term survival in selected patients.  

E. If the colorectal primary tumor has not yet been resected, schedule either a simultaneous colon resection (if technically feasible) or a staged colorectal surgery after hepatic recovery, based on operative risk and tumor location.  
   – Rationale: Primary tumor control is essential; simultaneous resection can be considered when operative time and patient condition allow.  

F. Continue postoperative/adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., maintenance bevacizumab or anti‑EGFR agents if later molecular profiling permits) and enroll in surveillance protocol (CEA, imaging every 3–6 months).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with liver metastases in segments IV, V, and VIII associated with a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis in the context of a left colon cancer. The presence of osseous metastatic disease indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control.

B. Management of bone metastasis
• Integrate radiotherapy and/or orthopedic evaluation for the right iliac lesion depending on symptoms and fracture risk.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform periodic liver MRI and whole-body imaging to monitor response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Role of liver-directed therapy
• Liver surgery is not indicated unless an exceptional systemic response with control of bone disease occurs, which remains unlikely.

E. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T3N1 rectal tumor with two liver metastases and an isolated left pulmonary nodule at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 210 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, possibility of a combined approach depending on response.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
• Rationale: The patient has only two liver metastases and a single isolated left‑lung nodule, which in principle can be addressed surgically if adequate hepatic functional reserve and pulmonary reserve are confirmed. However, critical data required to confirm technical resectability are missing (size and segmental location of liver lesions, relationship to major vessels or biliary structures, future liver remnant volume, size and anatomic relationship of the pulmonary nodule, and status of the rectal primary). Without these details the lesions cannot be definitively deemed resectable, but they are not obviously unresectable based on the limited disease burden described.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, PET‑CT, and pelvic MRI to define tumor biology, exact lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular involvement, FLR, and metabolic activity of the lung nodule.  
   – Perform pulmonary function tests and cardiopulmonary assessment.  
   Rationale: Precise anatomic and functional information is essential to plan curative‑intent surgery and to confirm that extra‑hepatic disease is truly limited.

B. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Initiate 3–4 cycles of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status.  
   Rationale: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy aims to down‑size hepatic and pulmonary lesions, treat micrometastatic disease, and provide a biologic test of tumor responsiveness.

C. Local treatment of the rectal primary  
   – If the rectal tumor has not yet been resected, deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) after systemic therapy, or consider a “watch‑and‑wait” approach only if complete clinical response is achieved.  
   Rationale: Optimal control of the primary rectal lesion is required before or concurrent with metastatic surgery to minimize local recurrence.

D. Restaging after induction therapy  
   – Repeat imaging (MRI, PET‑CT) to assess response of liver and lung lesions and to re‑evaluate resectability criteria (FLR, vascular clearance, pulmonary reserve).  
   Rationale: Decision for definitive surgery hinges on achieving resectable disease with adequate margins and functional reserve.

E. Curative‑intent metastasectomy (single or staged)  
   – If post‑therapy imaging shows resectable liver lesions with sufficient FLR (>30 % in a normal liver) and a resectable pulmonary nodule, proceed to combined or staged metastasectomy. Options:  
        • Simultaneous liver resection + pulmonary wedge resection (if operative time and patient condition permit).  
        • Staged approach: first liver resection, followed by pulmonary resection after recovery, or vice‑versa based on multidisciplinary consensus.  
   – Follow with adjuvant systemic therapy to complete a standard 6‑month total duration.  
   Rationale: Achieving R0 resection of all disease sites offers the best chance for long‑term survival in oligometastatic colorectal cancer.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Unresectable (current disease not amenable to curative‑intent surgery).  
- Justification:  
  • Eight bilobar liver metastases indicate diffuse hepatic involvement; the number and distribution exceed typical criteria for simultaneous or staged hepatic resection (generally ≤4 lesions confined to ≤2 segments with adequate future liver remnant).  
  • No data on lesion size, vascular or biliary invasion, but the presence of “moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis” adds extra‑hepatic disease that precludes an R0 liver‑only operation.  
  • The primary right‑colon tumor has not been reported as resected; without control of the primary lesion, curative liver surgery is not indicated.  
  • High CEA (970 ng/mL) suggests biologically aggressive disease.  
  • Absence of documented systemic therapy or down‑staging response further supports the unresectable status at this time.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive Restaging and Molecular Work‑up  
   - Obtain thoraco‑abdominal CT, liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, and FDG‑PET/CT to define extra‑hepatic burden (lung, bone, nodal).  
   - Perform colonoscopy to assess the primary lesion and obtain tissue for KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H status.  
   - Rationale: Precise anatomic and biologic data are required to select systemic regimen and to reassess resectability after treatment.  

B. Systemic Conversion Chemotherapy  
   - Initiate intensive first‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) or FOLFOX + bevacizumab if contraindications exist; consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy if RAS wild‑type.  
   - Rationale: Aim to achieve tumor shrinkage in liver and peritoneum, potentially converting to resectable status; also provides early control of occult disease.  

C. Re‑assessment After 2–3 months of Therapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI and CT of chest/abdomen; calculate peritoneal cancer index (PCI) if peritoneal disease persists.  
   - Rationale: Determine response (partial/complete) and evaluate whether hepatic FLR would be sufficient for resection; assess whether peritoneal disease has become limited enough for cytoreductive surgery ± HIPEC.  

D. Conditional Surgical Plan  
   - If conversion achieved (≤4 liver lesions confined to ≤2 segments with adequate FLR and PCI ≤10):  
        • Proceed with staged or simultaneous resection of primary colon tumor (right hemicolectomy) and curative liver resection; consider intra‑operative HIPEC if peritoneal disease remains limited.  
   - If conversion not achieved:  
        • Continue systemic therapy, consider enrollment in a clinical trial, and provide best supportive care/palliation as needed.  
   - Rationale: Surgery is reserved for patients who can attain an R0 resection of all disease sites; otherwise systemic therapy remains the mainstay.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases associated with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (970 ng/mL). The presence of peritoneal dissemination combined with extensive bilobar hepatic disease excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (970 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (technically resectable but requires optimization).  
- Justification:  
  • Five bilobar metastases, each ≤3.5 cm, which falls within conventional size limits for hepatic resection.  
  • Vascular contact limited to the middle hepatic vein (segment VIII lesion) without documented invasion; such contact can often be managed with careful parenchymal‑sparing techniques or vascular reconstruction.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; absence of pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases would meet the oncologic criteria for hepatic clearance.  
  • High CEA (1150 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive biology, suggesting the need for systemic disease control before definitive surgery.  
  • Missing data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve preclude immediate classification as “resectable” without further assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – Initiate 3–6 cycles of a KRAS‑mutant‑appropriate regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab). Rationale: down‑size lesions, treat micrometastatic disease, and assess tumor biology via CEA trend.  

B. Restaging work‑up – After chemotherapy, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and obtain performance status and liver function tests. Rationale: confirm response, detect occult extra‑hepatic disease, and calculate FLR volume.  

C. FLR optimization – If FLR <30 % (or <40 % in compromised liver), perform portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) based on volumetric results. Rationale: ensure adequate postoperative liver function.  

D. Surgical resection –  
   • If FLR adequate after PVE, proceed with a single‑stage, parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections of all five lesions, preserving the middle hepatic vein when possible; employ intra‑operative ultrasound for lesion localization.  
   • If FLR remains insufficient, adopt a two‑stage hepatectomy: first clear lesions in one lobe (often the left), perform PVE of the contralateral lobe, then complete right‑lobe resection after hypertrophy.  

E. Management of primary colon tumor –  
   • If the primary has not yet been resected, schedule a simultaneous colon resection during the liver operation only if operative time and patient condition permit; otherwise, perform colon resection in a separate, staged procedure after hepatic recovery.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Resume or continue chemotherapy post‑operatively (typically 3–6 additional cycles) to address residual microscopic disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (requires further evaluation).  
- Rationale: The patient has seven liver metastases ranging from 2 cm to 5 cm, which can be technically resected if they are distributed across segments that allow an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) and there is no major vascular or biliary invasion. Current imaging does not provide details on segmental distribution, vascular contact, or FLR volume, all of which are essential to determine operability. The absence of extra‑hepatic disease is favorable, but the aggressive BRAF V600E mutation and high CEA suggest a need for systemic down‑staging before surgery. Consequently, resectability cannot be confirmed at this stage; it remains potentially resectable pending additional data and response to neoadjuvant therapy.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Initiate systemic conversion therapy  
   - Action: Start intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with a BRAF‑targeted regimen (encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib) and bevacizumab.  
   - Rationale: BRAF‑mutated, MSS colorectal cancer has poor prognosis; upfront systemic therapy improves tumor shrinkage, may convert borderline liver disease to resectable status, and addresses micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging and detailed hepatic assessment (4–6 weeks after cycle 2)  
   - Action: Perform liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, volumetric CT for FLR calculation, and detailed vascular mapping (CT angiography).  
   - Rationale: Precise anatomic information is required to assess resectability, plan the extent of hepatectomy, and determine need for portal vein embolization (PVE) or staged approaches.  

C. Multidisciplinary decision point  
   - If imaging shows ≥ 30 % FLR (≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to surgical phase.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider PVE or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy before resection.  

D. Surgical phase (performed after primary colon tumor control)  
   1. Resection of the primary right‑colon tumor (segmental colectomy) – either before or concurrently with liver surgery depending on patient’s performance status and tumor symptoms.  
   2. Curative‑intent liver resection – either single‑stage anatomic/non‑anatomic resections or a two‑stage/ALPPS approach to achieve R0 margins while preserving adequate FLR.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy  
   - Action: Resume or continue BRAF‑targeted therapy with or without maintenance chemotherapy for at least 6 months post‑resection.  
   - Rationale: High risk of recurrence in BRAF‑mutated disease warrants continued systemic control.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, T3N2 upper rectal cancer with four liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 980 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases with MSI-H profile opening discussion for first-line immunotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (pending further data).  
- Rationale:  
  • Four liver metastases confined to the liver (no extra‑hepatic disease on current imaging).  
  • Bilobar distribution does not automatically preclude resection if lesions are amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resections with an adequate future liver remnant.  
  • Primary rectal tumor has not yet been resected, and its local stage (T3N2) requires neoadjuvant therapy before definitive surgery; therefore the patient cannot be declared resectable at this moment.  
  • Critical missing variables that determine technical resectability (size of each lesion, exact hepatic segments involved, relationship to major vessels or biliary structures, FLR volume, and response to systemic therapy) are not provided; consequently a definitive “resectable” or “unresectable” label cannot be assigned.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic therapy – first‑line immunotherapy  
   – Initiate pembrolizumab (or another PD‑1 inhibitor) given MSI‑H status, with or without a fluoropyrimidine‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) per current NCCN/ESMO recommendations for metastatic MSI‑H colorectal cancer.  
   – Goal: achieve tumor shrinkage in liver lesions and down‑stage the rectal primary.

B. Neoadjuvant chemoradiation for the rectal primary  
   – Deliver long‑course pelvic radiotherapy (50.4 Gy) with concurrent capecitabine or 5‑FU.  
   – Aim: improve local control, increase the chance of sphincter‑preserving resection, and potentially allow a watch‑and‑wait approach if complete clinical response occurs.

C. Restaging after 8–12 weeks of systemic therapy  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and volumetric analysis.  
   – Re‑evaluate number, size, and vascular involvement of hepatic lesions; calculate FLR ratio.  
   – Re‑stage the rectal tumor with pelvic MRI and endoscopic assessment.

D. Liver‑directed surgery (if restaging confirms resectability)  
   – If all lesions can be cleared with an FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to curative liver resection.  
   – Options: (i) one‑stage anatomic/segmental resections if feasible; (ii) staged approach (e.g., portal vein embolization followed by resection) if FLR is insufficient; (iii) consider ablative techniques for lesions in difficult locations.  

E. Definitive management of the rectal primary  
   – If a complete clinical response is documented, discuss a non‑operative watch‑and‑wait strategy.  
   – If residual disease persists, perform low anterior resection (or abdominoperineal resection if required) after hepatic surgery, ensuring adequate oncologic margins.  

F. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   – Continue pembrolizumab for up to 2 years or until disease progression, per guideline‑based duration.  
   – Consider additional adjuvant chemotherapy based on pathological response and multidisciplinary consensus.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, two liver metastases segments II and III (3.2 and 4.0 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 320 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 positive.
MDT Discussion: Limited involvement but HER2 mutation may influence systemic therapeutic strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable.  
• Rationale:  
  – Liver disease is limited to two lesions (3.2 cm and 4.0 cm) confined to segments II and III, which can be removed by a left‑lateral segmentectomy while preserving a sufficient future liver remnant (right liver).  
  – No imaging evidence of vascular, biliary, or major hepatic structure invasion is reported.  
  – No documented extra‑hepatic metastases; however, thoracic imaging has not been performed, so distant disease cannot be excluded.  
  – Primary colon tumor has not yet been resected; its status must be clarified before definitive surgical planning.  
  – Assuming adequate performance status and liver function, the hepatic component meets current criteria for curative intent resection, pending confirmation of absent extra‑hepatic disease and assessment of FLR.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete Staging  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate lesion borders, vascular relationships, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   – Endoscopic evaluation of the primary colon lesion to assess for obstruction, perforation, or bleeding and to obtain histologic grade.  

B. Primary Tumor Management  
   – If the primary lesion is symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) or high‑risk, proceed with oncologic resection (segmental colectomy) first; otherwise, schedule simultaneous or staged resection after systemic therapy.  

C. Systemic Therapy (Neoadjuvant)  
   – Initiate HER2‑directed doublet therapy (trastuzumab + pertuzumab) combined with standard chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) given HER2 positivity and high CEA.  
   – Aim to treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially downsize liver lesions.  

D. Re‑assessment and Liver Resection  
   – Restage after 2–3 months of systemic therapy with repeat liver MRI and thoracic imaging.  
   – If disease remains limited to the liver and FLR is adequate, perform curative left‑lateral segmentectomy (segments II/III).  
   – Consider simultaneous colon and liver resection if the primary is resected and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits; otherwise, stage the procedures (colon first, then liver 4–6 weeks later).  

E. Post‑operative Consolidation  
   – Continue HER2‑targeted therapy with or without chemotherapy for a total of 6–12 months, tailored to response and tolerability.  
   – Implement surveillance with serial CEA, cross‑sectional imaging, and colonoscopy per guidelines.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, nine bilobar metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2500 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.Liver  MRI: infiltration of the right portal pedicle.
MDT Discussion: Major liver involvement, vascular invasion compromising resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline) after conversion therapy.  
- Justification:  
  • Nine bilobar liver metastases indicate extensive hepatic disease.  
  • MRI shows infiltration of the right portal pedicle, representing major vascular involvement that currently precludes a safe anatomic resection with adequate future liver remnant.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT, which preserves the possibility of curative intent.  
  • High CEA (2500 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest aggressive biology but do not rule out down‑staging.  
  • Because the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and segmental distribution are not provided, the technical feasibility of a one‑stage resection cannot be confirmed at this time.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   – Regimen: FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).  
   – Rationale: Aim to achieve tumor shrinkage, reduce vascular invasion, and possibly convert disease to resectable status.  

B. Restaging after 2–3 months of therapy  
   – Perform repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT of chest/abdomen.  
   – Rationale: Assess response of hepatic lesions, degree of portal pedicle involvement, and calculate FLR volume.  

C. If adequate response and FLR <30 % of total liver volume, perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branch  
   – Rationale: Induce hypertrophy of the left liver to secure a safe FLR for subsequent resection.  

D. Surgical resection (timing based on response)  
   – If disease is down‑staged to ≤4 lesions with clear margins and adequate FLR, proceed to curative hepatectomy (potentially a staged or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS, if rapid hypertrophy is needed).  
   – Simultaneously perform primary colon resection (right hemicolectomy) if not already done, provided the patient is fit.  
   – Rationale: Achieve R0 resection of both primary tumor and liver metastases.  

E. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Continue adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX) for at least 6 months.  
   – Rationale: Reduce risk of recurrence given high baseline CEA and aggressive pathology.

The combination of extensive bilobar disease and portal pedicle involvement precludes the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2500 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)

• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response and reassess vascular relationships.

• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major response occurs with regression of portal pedicle involvement and significant reduction in tumor burden.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective and dependent on restoration of clear vascular anatomy.

• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 61 years old, T3N1M1 rectal tumor, three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII). CEA 680 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: extension to the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Metastases near venous confluence, high surgical risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
• Rationale:  
  – Three hepatic lesions confined to segments IVa, VI and VIII meet the numeric criteria for resection.  
  – Presence of vascular contact/invasion at the hepatic‑vein confluence raises technical complexity and may require major hepatectomy or venous reconstruction, but does not automatically preclude resection.  
  – No documented extra‑hepatic disease; if truly absent, liver‑only disease remains a surgical indication.  
  – Critical data needed to confirm resectability (size of lesions, future liver remnant volume, arterial anatomy, liver function, performance status) are missing; therefore the case is considered potentially resectable pending further assessment and possible down‑staging with systemic therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and 3‑D reconstruction to define lesion size, relationship to hepatic veins, arterial anatomy, and to calculate FLR.  
   – Endoscopic evaluation of the rectal primary; if not yet resected, stage with MRI pelvis.  
   – Rationale: Complete anatomic and functional mapping is essential before committing to surgery and to plan possible portal vein embolization or venous reconstruction.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (conversion)  
   – Initiate a standard oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS mutation (anti‑EGFR agents ineffective).  
   – Treat for 2–3 months with radiologic reassessment.  
   – Rationale: Aim to achieve tumor shrinkage, improve resectability of the hepatic‑vein confluence lesion, and treat micrometastatic disease.  

C. Management of the rectal primary  
   – If the primary tumor has not been resected, deliver long‑course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (capecitabine‑based) followed by restaging.  
   – Plan low anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving surgery) after systemic therapy, preferably before or concurrently with liver surgery depending on operative risk.  
   – Rationale: Control of the primary tumor reduces risk of local complications and aligns with oncologic sequencing (primary first when feasible).  

D. Liver surgery (post‑systemic therapy)  
   – Re‑evaluate imaging after systemic therapy; if adequate response and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % in steatotic liver), proceed to hepatic resection.  
   – Preferred approach: parenchymal‑sparing resections of segments VI and VIII combined with a segment IVa resection; if venous involvement persists, consider right trisectionectomy with hepatic‑vein reconstruction or portal vein embolization pre‑operatively to augment FLR.  
   – Rationale: Achieve R0 resection while preserving sufficient liver volume; vascular reconstruction is justified only when oncologic clearance is attainable.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., continuation of bevacizumab‑containing regimen) for 3–6 months post‑resection.  
   – Follow with serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  
   – Rationale: Consolidate response, address residual microscopic disease, and monitor for recurrence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII) with MRI showing extension toward the hepatic vein confluence. Although the number of lesions is limited, their proximity to the venous outflow confluence makes a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate hepatic venous drainage technically uncertain. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely tumor downsizing.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (680 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA (680 ng/mL), KRAS mutation, and complex vascular location, initiate 3–6 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Expert vascular restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate venous outflow preservation or need for reconstruction.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If sufficient tumor regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections, or standard anatomic major hepatectomy with or without vascular reconstruction aiming for R0 margins.

E. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Four bilobar liver metastases indicate disease amenable to hepatic clearance if sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • The lesion in segment VII invades the inferior vena cava (IVC) over >1 cm, representing major vascular involvement that can be addressed only with complex IVC resection/reconstruction; this does not automatically preclude resection but requires vascular surgical expertise and careful patient selection.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; however, absence of staging imaging (chest/abdomen CT) precludes definitive confirmation of isolated hepatic disease.  
  • Primary colorectal tumor status unknown; synchronous resection may be required.  
  • Adequate FLR and vascular anatomy have not been reported; these are essential to deem the case resectable.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy  
   - Initiate combination chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology, attempt down‑staging of liver lesions, and treat occult micrometastatic disease.  
B. Restaging and comprehensive staging  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis; repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast; obtain PET‑CT if indicated to rule out extra‑hepatic metastases and to evaluate response of the IVC‑invasive lesion.  
C. Multidisciplinary surgical planning  
   - If imaging confirms disease limited to liver and the IVC invasion remains resectable, convene hepatobiliary‑vascular team to plan:  
     • Simultaneous or staged colon resection (if primary not yet removed).  
     • Liver resection with en‑bloc IVC segmental resection and prosthetic or autologous reconstruction, ensuring negative margins.  
     • Intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion borders and assess additional occult disease.  
D. FLR optimization and operative sequencing  
   - Calculate FLR volume; if <30 % in a normal liver or <40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to augment FLR before definitive resection.  
   - Proceed to definitive hepatic resection once adequate FLR and patient fitness are confirmed.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases, including a segment VII lesion invading the IVC over ~1 cm, without reported extrahepatic disease. While the number of lesions is limited, true caval invasion makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unlikely without complex vascular resection/reconstruction and carries high operative risk. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only in a highly selected setting, after tumor downsizing and multidisciplinary vascular assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (900 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with or without partial IVC resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with vascular surgery is required to assess feasibility of partial IVC resection/reconstruction if needed.

C. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• One or two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• If regression of caval invasion occurs or reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of all lesions.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or graft reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, five liver metastases including one 8.5 cm in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 870 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis with bilateral portal contact, complex technical discussion.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Five hepatic lesions, including an 8.5 cm central metastasis in segment IVb with bilateral portal vein contact, indicate a high tumor burden and technically demanding resection.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on current imaging.  
  • Absence of data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, portal vein anatomy, and response to systemic therapy prevents a definitive “resectable” label.  
  • Current hepatobiliary criteria consider such cases potentially resectable after down‑staging chemotherapy and/or FLR augmentation (e.g., portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy).  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
   - Goal: tumor shrinkage, control of micrometastatic disease, and assessment of biologic response (CEA trend).  

B. Comprehensive restaging (4–6 weeks after systemic therapy)  
   - Perform liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT‑angiography to delineate arterial and portal anatomy, lesion response, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   - Re‑evaluate for any occult extra‑hepatic disease (including brain MRI if clinically indicated).  

C. Optimization of hepatic reserve  
   - If FLR is <30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the diseased lobe or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS approach.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - If the primary has not yet been resected, schedule colectomy either simultaneously with liver resection (if operative risk acceptable) or as a staged procedure after hepatic down‑staging, based on symptomatology and oncologic urgency.  

E. Definitive liver surgery  
   - Aim for an R0 resection of all hepatic metastases using an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing technique, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound.  
   - Consider combined right and left hepatectomy, extended left hepatectomy, or staged resections depending on FLR adequacy and intra‑operative findings.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Continue postoperative chemotherapy (potentially with maintenance bevacizumab) to address residual microscopic disease.
