Case_Content:
Man, 73 years old, transverse colon tumor, two liver metastases (4.2 and 4.8 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 70 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Normal CEA despite high volume, question regarding biological sensitivity for follow-up.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable.  
• Rationale: The patient has two liver metastases, each ≤5 cm, which meets the size and number criteria for hepatic resection. No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on the available thoraco‑abdominal CT. However, critical information required to confirm technical resectability is missing – specifically the hepatic segments involved, presence or absence of major vascular or biliary invasion, and the future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio. Without these data the lesions cannot be declared unequivocally resectable, but they are not outright unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete restaging and functional imaging  
   – Obtain a liver‑specific MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) to delineate segmental distribution, vascular relationships, and to calculate FLR.  
   – Consider a PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases (particularly brain, bone, or peritoneum).  
   – Rationale: Precise anatomic mapping and confirmation of disease‑free extra‑hepatic sites are mandatory before committing to curative surgery.

B. Management of the primary colorectal lesion  
   – If the transverse colon tumor has not yet been resected, schedule a curative‑intent colectomy (segmental resection with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
   – This can be performed either before or simultaneously with liver surgery, depending on the patient’s performance status and operative risk.  
   – Rationale: Primary tumor control is essential; simultaneous resection is feasible in selected patients and may shorten overall treatment time.

C. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Initiate peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS/BRAF wild‑type status).  
   – Re‑evaluate tumor response after 2–3 months with repeat imaging.  
   – Rationale: Down‑staging may improve resectability margins, allow assessment of tumor biology (response predicts outcome), and treat micrometastatic disease early.

D. Curative‑intent liver resection  
   – If post‑chemotherapy imaging confirms adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % if steatosis/fibrosis) and no vascular invasion, proceed with parenchymal‑sparing resection (segmental or wedge) aiming for R0 margins.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to verify lesion location and margins.  
   – Rationale: Achieving negative margins while preserving liver function offers the best chance for long‑term survival.

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Resume or complete a total of 6–8 months of systemic chemotherapy after hepatic surgery, tailored to response and tolerability.  
   – Rationale: Consolidates disease control and addresses potential residual microscopic disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (4.2 and 4.8 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. Both lesions are limited in number and appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± cetuximab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if major hepatectomy is considered.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Management of the primary tumor
• Either combined or staged transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, left T4N1M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 1400 ng/mL. KRAS G12C mutation confirmed.
MDT Discussion: Specific molecular profile, may benefit from a later targeted strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification: The patient has six liver metastases with a maximum diameter of 5.6 cm, which exceeds the ideal “≤4 cm or ≤3 lesions” criteria for straightforward upfront resection. Absence of documented vascular invasion, FLR calculation, and extra‑hepatic disease prevents a definitive “resectable” label. However, no proven extra‑hepatic metastases are reported, and modern conversion chemotherapy can down‑size disease, making a curative intent surgery feasible in many similar cases. Therefore the lesions are considered potentially resectable pending further assessment and systemic therapy response.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion therapy  
   - Initiate an intensive first‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) combined with a KRAS‑G12C targeted agent (sotorasib or adagrasib) once eligibility is confirmed.  
   - Rationale: Down‑size hepatic disease, treat occult micrometastases, and exploit the known KRAS‑G12C mutation for added response.

B. Comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, chest CT (or PET‑CT), and repeat abdominal CT.  
   - Assess: number and distribution of lesions, vascular/biliary involvement, future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and any newly evident extra‑hepatic sites.  
   - Rationale: Determine whether sufficient tumor shrinkage and an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % if steatosis/fibrosis) have been achieved to permit safe resection.

C. Surgical planning (based on restaging)  
   - If disease is confined to the liver and FLR is adequate: proceed with simultaneous or staged curative hepatectomy (e.g., anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing resections; consider two‑stage or ALPPS only if FLR is marginal).  
   - If the primary colon tumor remains unresected and symptomatic or at risk for obstruction, perform co‑ordinated colon resection (either simultaneous with liver surgery if operative risk is acceptable, or staged before/after hepatic resection).  
   - Rationale: Achieve R0 resection of all macroscopic disease while preserving sufficient liver function.

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume systemic therapy (including KRAS‑G12C inhibitor) post‑operatively for a minimum of 6 months, tailored to pathologic response and margin status.  
   - Implement surveillance protocol: CEA every 3 months, contrast CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   - Rationale: Reduce recurrence risk and detect early metastatic spread.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) in the context of a left T4N1 colon cancer and very high CEA (1400 ng/mL). The number, size, and likely bilobar distribution of lesions make a safe R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant unlikely at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (1400 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The presence of a KRAS G12C mutation is poor prognostic factor and may allow consideration of targeted strategies in later lines of therapy. 
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major radiologic and biologic response occurs with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections.

E. Management of the primary tumor
• Consider transverse colectomy of right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis if the tumor is symptomatic of if MDT propose intra-arterial chemotherapy.

F. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• If disease remains extensive, consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, low T3N2M1 rectal cancer, four peripheral liver metastases (2-3.5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 90 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS, positive circulating tumor cells.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating cells despite low volume, prognostic significance discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale: The patient has four peripheral liver metastases, each ≤3.5 cm, which generally meet size and number criteria for hepatic resection. No imaging evidence of major vascular or biliary invasion is reported, and there is no documented extra‑hepatic disease. However, critical data required to confirm technical resectability are missing (hepatic segments involved, relationship to portal/hepatic veins, arterial anatomy, and future liver remnant (FLR) volumetry). Until these are clarified, the lesions can be considered potentially resectable but not definitively resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary  
   - Rationale: T3N2 rectal cancer warrants long‑course chemoradiation to achieve down‑staging, improve sphincter preservation, and reduce local recurrence risk before definitive surgery.  

B. Systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody)  
   - Rationale: Stage IV disease with circulating tumor cells indicates high systemic burden. RAS‑wild‑type status allows use of anti‑EGFR therapy, which may increase response rates and facilitate conversion of liver metastases to resectable status.  

C. Restaging with high‑resolution liver MRI and volumetric CT  
   - Rationale: Precise mapping of metastatic distribution, assessment of vascular involvement, and calculation of FLR are essential to plan a safe hepatic resection and to decide between simultaneous versus staged approach.  

D. Surgical resection (sequence based on restaging results)  
   - If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % after chemotherapy) and no major vascular invasion: proceed with simultaneous resection (total mesorectal excision + anatomic liver resection) in a single operation.  
   - If FLR insufficient or major vascular contact is present: adopt a staged approach – first complete the rectal resection (after neoadjuvant chemoradiation), then perform portal vein embolization or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) or conventional two‑stage hepatectomy to achieve adequate FLR before definitive liver resection.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy (post‑operative)  
   - Rationale: To eradicate microscopic residual disease and address any remaining circulating tumor cells, continue systemic chemotherapy for a total of 6‑12 months, adjusting regimen based on pathologic response and tolerability.
Reference:

The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (2–3.5 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. Case_Content:
Woman, 68 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥10 lesions) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2700 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Massive liver disease with high marker elevation, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current classification: Potentially resectable after down‑staging (not immediately resectable).  
- Justification:  
  • ≥10 hepatic lesions – exceeds the typical threshold for upfront curative hepatectomy.  
  • Distribution of lesions, segmental involvement, vascular or biliary invasion, and future liver remnant (FLR) are unknown, preventing confirmation of technical resectability.  
  • Primary right‑sided T4N2 tumor remains unresected, which is a prerequisite for any curative intent strategy.  
  • Very high CEA (2700 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive biology, supporting the need for systemic disease control before surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab).  
   - Rationale: Aim to shrink hepatic disease, reduce lesion number, and assess tumor biology; KRAS‑mutated disease still responds to intensive regimens.  

B. Restaging with high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted imaging) and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT after 2–3 months of therapy.  
   - Rationale: Precise mapping of residual lesions, assessment of vascular involvement, and calculation of FLR to determine operability.  

C. Multidisciplinary decision point based on restaging:  
   - If ≤4 lesions confined to ≤2 liver segments with adequate FLR (≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), proceed to curative surgery.  
   - Surgical plan:  
     • First, right hemicolectomy (primary tumor resection) with oncologic lymphadenectomy.  
     • Second, staged liver resection (major hepatectomy or parenchymal‑sparing resection combined with intra‑operative ablation) performed 4–6 weeks after colectomy, provided patient fitness and liver function are acceptable.  

D. If down‑staging is insufficient (still >4 lesions, inadequate FLR, or unresectable vascular involvement):  
   - Continue systemic therapy, consider enrollment in a clinical trial, or discuss best‑supportive care according to patient wishes and performance status.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with ≥10 liver metastases in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and very high CEA (2700 ng/mL). The tumor burden, multiplicity of lesions, and likely bilobar distribution preclude the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2700 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in the rare situation of major radiologic and biologic response with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections.

D. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer at the abdominal CT scan, three liver metastases (2-3 cm) and confirmed left portal invasion on liver MRI. CEA 310 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Unilateral portal involvement, potentially approachable depending on volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Three liver metastases each ≤3 cm, which is within conventional size limits for hepatic resection.  
  • Unilateral left‑portal vein involvement is noted; such vascular involvement can be addressed with portal vein resection/reconstruction or with portal vein embolization to augment future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease on imaging; however, thoracic imaging has not been performed, so distant metastases cannot be excluded.  
  • Resectability hinges on adequate FLR, arterial anatomy, and confirmation that the primary colon lesion can be controlled; these data are currently missing.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Perform colonoscopy if not already done to assess the primary lesion and obtain biopsies for molecular profiling.  

B. Primary tumor control  
   – If the left‑sided colon primary has not been resected, schedule a curative‑intent colectomy (segmental resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) either before or simultaneously with liver surgery, depending on patient fitness and tumor symptoms.  

C. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of modern combination chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology, potentially downsize the portal‑vein–involved lesion, and treat occult micrometastatic disease.  
   – Re‑evaluate CEA trend and radiologic response after induction.  

D. Re‑assessment of hepatic resectability  
   – Repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to quantify FLR volume, delineate arterial and portal anatomy, and confirm extent of vascular involvement.  
   – If FLR is <30 % in a normal liver (or <40 % after chemotherapy), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to induce hypertrophy.  

E. Definitive hepatic surgery (planned after systemic therapy and FLR optimization)  
   – Perform an anatomic left hepatectomy with en‑bloc resection of the involved left portal vein segment, followed by portal vein reconstruction.  
   – If intra‑operative assessment shows adequate margins, consider simultaneous colon resection; otherwise, stage the procedures.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Continue postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months total cumulative) based on response and molecular profile.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases (2–3 cm) associated with confirmed left portal vein invasion on MRI, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is limited, portal involvement compromises the feasibility of a safe R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and precise volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 3 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (310 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (310 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS status is unknown
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.

D. Surgical management of liver metastases
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first left hepatectomy with parenchymal-sparing liver resection of the remaining lesions aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Management of primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 150 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, right T3N0M1 colon tumor, single 5.6 cm metastasis in segment VIII, in close contact with IVC at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 540 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis, major technical question regarding surgical approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (requires further evaluation).  
- Rationale:  
  • Single hepatic lesion, 5.6 cm, confined to segment VIII – meets size and number criteria for hepatic resection.  
  • No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone negative).  
  • RAS wild‑type status favors responsiveness to systemic therapy and possible conversion to resectability.  
  • Close contact with the inferior vena cava raises technical concerns (possible IVC involvement, need for vascular control or reconstruction) but does not automatically preclude resection.  
  • Adequate future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be confirmed because volumetric data are missing; therefore resectability remains “potential” pending FLR assessment and liver function evaluation.  
  • Primary colon tumor has not yet been resected; simultaneous or staged resection must be planned after confirming hepatic feasibility.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction therapy (e.g., 2–3 months of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab)  
   – Rationale: Down‑size the liver lesion, treat occult micrometastases, and assess tumor biology before committing to major surgery.  

B. Restaging work‑up after induction  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase, CT‑angiography for arterial/portal anatomy, volumetric CT to calculate FLR, and assessment of IVC involvement (extent of contact, need for vascular reconstruction).  
   – Rationale: Precise anatomic mapping and functional reserve are essential to determine whether an R0 hepatic resection is technically feasible and safe.  

C. Surgical plan (contingent on restaging results)  
   1. If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) and IVC involvement is limited to adventitial contact, proceed with curative intent:  
      – Right hemicolectomy (primary tumor) performed either simultaneously with liver resection or as a staged procedure, depending on operative risk and anticipated liver‑only operative time.  
      – Segment VIII anatomical resection (or extended right hepatectomy) with vascular control; if IVC invasion is confirmed, plan for limited IVC resection and primary repair or patch graft.  
   2. If FLR is insufficient or IVC invasion is extensive, consider:  
      – Portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy FLR, followed by delayed hepatic resection.  
      – Alternative local therapy (e.g., percutaneous ablation) if surgical margins are unlikely to be negative.  

D. Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance) for at least 6 months.  
   – Rationale: Consolidate response, reduce recurrence risk, especially given high pre‑operative CEA.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 5.6 cm liver metastasis in segment VIII in close contact with the IVC, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although solitary, the central location and caval proximity make a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection technically demanding and potentially unsafe without prior tumor downsizing or vascular planning. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely induction therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of the lesion with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (540 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and hepatic veins.
• If regression occurs or vascular control is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or reconstruction with multidisciplinary discussion with vascular surgery to assess feasibility of tangential IVC resection if needed.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Management of primary tumor
• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 69 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma, six liver metastases (1.5-4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 850 ng/mL, BRAF V600E mutation.
MDT Discussion: Unfavorable molecular profile, bilobar liver involvement with systemic potential.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (not outright resectable, not unresectable).  
- Rationale: Six bilobar metastases (1.5‑4 cm) can be technically resected if adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be achieved and there is no major vascular or biliary invasion. Current imaging lacks detail on segmental distribution, vascular contact, and FLR volume, which are essential to confirm that an R0 resection with sufficient liver reserve is feasible. The presence of a BRAF V600E mutation and markedly elevated CEA (850 ng/mL) indicate aggressive biology, favoring neoadjuvant systemic therapy to improve oncologic outcomes before any surgical attempt.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging – Obtain liver‑specific MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging and volumetric analysis, plus PET‑CT if not already performed, to define segmental involvement, vascular/biliary relationships, and to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (including brain).  
B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – Initiate an intensive regimen appropriate for BRAF‑mutated colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with anti‑EGFR therapy plus a BRAF inhibitor such as encorafenib). Goal: tumor down‑staging, CEA reduction, and assessment of treatment response.  
C. Re‑assessment of resectability – After 2–3 months of systemic therapy, repeat imaging and FLR volumetry. If ≥30 % FLR (≥40 % after chemotherapy) and no major vascular encasement, proceed to surgery.  
D. Surgical phase – Perform simultaneous or staged resection depending on intra‑operative assessment:  
   - If primary tumor remains unresected and symptomatic, consider a “colon first” approach (segmental colectomy) followed by liver resection within the same operation or within 2–4 weeks.

- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Four hepatic lesions meet the numeric criteria for resection, and no extra‑hepatic disease has been documented.  
  • RAS wild‑type and MSI‑high status favor responsiveness to systemic therapy, increasing the chance of down‑staging to a resectable state.  
  • Definitive resectability cannot be confirmed because critical anatomic details are missing (size of each lesion, hepatic segmental distribution, relationship to major vessels/ biliary structures, and future liver remnant volume).

   – Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, chest CT (or PET‑CT), and full body imaging to define lesion size, segmental involvement, vascular contact, and to rule out occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Calculate FLR and assess hepatic functional reserve (e.g., ICG clearance, volumetry).  

B. Systemic induction therapy  
   – Initiate first‑line immunotherapy (pembrolizumab) given MSI‑H status, combined with a fluoropyrimidine‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) to maximize tumor shrinkage of both primary and liver lesions.  
   – Rationale: MSI‑H tumors have high response rates to checkpoint inhibition; adding chemotherapy improves conversion rates for liver metastases.

   – Repeat liver MRI and chest imaging to evaluate radiologic response and re‑calculate FLR.  
   – If all hepatic lesions have regressed to ≤3 cm and are amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resection with an adequate FLR (≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy), proceed to surgery.

   – If the rectal primary remains symptomatic or at risk for local complications, perform neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by total mesorectal excision (TME).

   – Rationale: Combined or staged approach is dictated by operative risk, tumor burden, and response; simultaneous resection is feasible when liver disease is limited and FLR is adequate.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   – Continue pembrolizumab for a total of 2 years or until disease progression, per current guidelines for MSI‑H colorectal cancer.  
   – Consider adjuvant chemotherapy if pathology shows high‑risk features.

- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Eight bilobar liver metastases exceed the conventional “≤4 lesions” threshold for straightforward resection.  
  • Contact with the right hepatic vein indicates major vascular involvement, raising the risk of insufficient margins and postoperative liver failure.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume or hepatic arterial/portal anatomy, which are essential to confirm that a safe hepatic resection can be achieved.  
  • High CEA (1300 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation are adverse biological factors, suggesting aggressive disease.  
  • The MDT notes “significant operative risk,” reflecting concerns about patient fitness and technical complexity.  
  • Because down‑staging with systemic therapy may reduce tumor burden and allow portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy, the case is not deemed outright unresectable but requires conversion treatment first.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy

   – Administer intensive conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to attempt tumor shrinkage and assess biologic response.  
   – Rationale: High tumor burden, KRAS mutation, and elevated CEA favor aggressive systemic treatment to improve resectability odds.

   – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and volumetric CT to:  
        • Measure residual lesion size, number, and vascular involvement.  
        • Calculate FLR volume and assess hepatic arterial/portal anatomy.  
   – Rationale: Determines whether a curative‑intent hepatic resection is feasible and guides need for portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS.  

C. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   – If the primary lesion has not yet been resected and is asymptomatic, plan for simultaneous or staged colectomy after systemic therapy response, depending on operative risk and liver surgery timing.  
   – Rationale: Primary tumor control is required before or concurrent with liver surgery to prevent future complications.

        • Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy with PVE to hypertrophy the future remnant, followed by completion hepatectomy.  
        • Alternatively, if rapid hypertrophy is needed and patient fitness permits, an ALPPS procedure may be contemplated.  
   – If margins remain inadequate despite down‑staging, proceed to best‑available systemic therapy and consider locoregional options (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion, radio‑embolization) for disease control.  
   – Rationale: Staged hepatic resection maximizes curative potential while preserving adequate liver function; ALPPS offers faster hypertrophy but carries higher morbidity, suitable only for selected patients.  

E. Post‑operative/adjuvant therapy  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (potentially with different agents) after hepatic surgery to eradicate microscopic disease.  
   – Rationale: High recurrence risk in KRAS‑mutated, high‑CEA disease warrants continued systemic control.

   - If the left‑sided colon primary has not been resected, schedule oncologic colectomy (segmental resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) before or concurrently with systemic therapy, ensuring no obstruction, perforation, or active bleeding.

From a purely technical hepatobiliary standpoint, the number and size of lesions could allow parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. This situation is therefore technically potentially resectable. However, the presence of a POLE mutation indicates a hypermutated, potentially immuno-sensitive tumor biology that strongly influences the therapeutic sequence.

A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the biological discordance of CEA level (400 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. First-line systemic immunotherapy (preferred strategy)
• Given the POLE mutation and hypermutated profile, initiate immunotherapy according to MDT decision.
• The objective is major tumor regression and assessment of tumor biology before considering surgery.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical re-evaluation after response
• If residual lesions persist after a major response, reassess segmental resectability.
• Plan ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections only if complete clearance is feasible with adequate future liver remnant.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, seven liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1150 ng/mL, NRAS Q61R mutation.
MDT Discussion: Specific NRAS molecular profile, no sensitivity to anti-EGFR.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (requires further evaluation).  
- Rationale: The patient has a solitary primary transverse colon cancer (T4N2) with seven hepatic lesions. Current data lack critical details on lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, and future liver remnant (FLR) volume. Absence of documented extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic imaging also limits certainty. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, multiple liver metastases can be resected if they are confined to segments that allow an adequate FLR (≥20‑30 % in a normal liver) and no unresectable extra‑hepatic disease is present. Because these parameters are missing, the case cannot be declared outright resectable or unresectable; it remains potentially resectable pending complete staging and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (including lung bases) and a liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and to detect occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR and assess portal venous anatomy.  
   - Evaluate performance status, baseline liver function tests, and comorbidities.  

B. Systemic conversion therapy  
   - Initiate a standard first‑line regimen for RAS‑mutated metastatic colorectal cancer, e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab, or FOLFOX ± bevacizumab if tolerance is a concern.  
   - Rationale: anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective with NRAS Q61R; intensive chemotherapy aims to downsize hepatic disease and treat potential microscopic extra‑hepatic disease, increasing the chance of curative resection.  

C. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months of chemotherapy  
   - Repeat imaging (CT/MRI) to evaluate radiologic response, FLR adequacy, and any new extra‑hepatic lesions.  
   - If disease is down‑staged to ≤4 resectable lesions with a satisfactory FLR, proceed to curative surgery.  

D. Surgical phase (curative intent)  
   - Primary tumor: Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy (or extended transverse colectomy) first, unless obstructive symptoms dictate urgent resection.  
   - Liver: Depending on FLR, choose one‑stage anatomical or non‑anatomical resections; if FLR is insufficient, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS).  
   - Rationale: Simultaneous resection is feasible when operative risk is acceptable and FLR is adequate; staged approaches preserve liver function when extensive resections are needed.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (potentially with maintenance bevacizumab) after postoperative recovery, tailored to pathologic response and residual disease risk.  
   - Implement surveillance with periodic CEA measurement and imaging per guidelines.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven liver metastases in the setting of a T4N2 transverse colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (1150 ng/mL). The number of lesions and likely bilobar distribution make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The NRAS Q61R mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major radiologic and biologic response occurs with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections with R0 margin.

E. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform extended right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right and transverse colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

G. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 70 years old, left colon tumor, three liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 200 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. MRI: invasion of the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular involvement, significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Three synchronous liver metastases meet the numeric criteria for resection.  
  • RAS wild‑type status and absence of extra‑hepatic disease are favorable.  
  • Invasion of the hepatic vein confluence represents major vascular involvement that raises technical complexity and may jeopardize an R0 margin or adequate outflow, but does not automatically preclude resection.  
  • Critical data required to confirm feasibility (future liver remnant volume, exact segmental distribution, arterial/portal anatomy, and functional liver reserve) are missing; therefore the case remains potentially resectable pending further assessment and possible down‑staging.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate a modern doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type.  
   - Goals: tumor down‑staging, assessment of biological behavior, and treatment of occult micrometastases.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment  
   - After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and CT‑based volumetry.  
   - Determine FLR ratio, exact hepatic segments involved, and re‑evaluate vascular invasion.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  

C. Surgical resection  
   - If adequate FLR is achieved and imaging shows resectable disease with clear margins, proceed to liver resection.  
   - Options include an extended right or left hepatectomy with reconstruction of the hepatic vein confluence (e.g., interposition graft or patch) or a staged two‑step approach (first clearing one lobe, then the second after hypertrophy).  
   - Simultaneous or sequential resection of the primary colon tumor should be performed once the patient is optimized; if the primary has not yet been removed, consider a combined colon resection and liver surgery in the same operative session if operative risk is acceptable, otherwise stage colon resection first.  

D. Adjuvant therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume postoperative systemic therapy (potentially the same regimen) for 3–6 months, tailored to response and tolerance.  
   - Follow with serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for at least 3 years.
Reference:

The patient presents with three liver metastases and MRI evidence of invasion of the hepatic vein confluence, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is limited, involvement of the venous outflow confluence makes a safe R0 resection with preservation of adequate hepatic venous drainage technically uncertain at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert vascular reassessment.

A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and potential reduction of venous involvement.

• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.

• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate feasibility of venous preservation or need for reconstruction.

• If significant regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable.  
• Rationale:  
  – Four liver metastases (3–5 cm) are present, described as bilobar, which can be addressed with modern hepatic surgery (multiple‑segmental or staged resections).  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on imaging (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone assumed absent).  
  – Adequate oncologic criteria (ability to achieve R0 margins, preservation of sufficient future liver remnant) cannot be confirmed because data on segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, and FLR volumetry are missing.  
  – The primary colon tumor has not yet been resected, and the patient’s performance status and liver functional reserve are unknown; therefore definitive resectability cannot be affirmed without further assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – Initiate an effective chemotherapy regimen for BRAF‑mutated colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or a doublet with anti‑VEGF) to down‑size hepatic lesions, treat occult micrometastases, and assess tumor biology.  
B. Restaging and functional assessment – After 2–3 cycles, obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging, perform volumetric CT for future liver remnant (FLR) calculation, and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT to confirm absence of new extra‑hepatic disease. Evaluate vascular and biliary involvement and consider portal vein embolization if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy).  
C. Surgical resection –  
   1. Primary tumor – Perform right hemicolectomy (open or laparoscopic) either concurrently with liver surgery if operative risk is acceptable and FLR is adequate, or as a separate staged procedure if liver surgery will be extensive.  
   2. Liver metastases – Execute curative‑intent liver resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing) aiming for R0 margins; choose simultaneous or staged hepatectomy based on FLR, lesion distribution, and intra‑operative assessment.  
D. Adjuvant/Consolidation therapy – Resume or continue systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively (typically 3–6 months) to eradicate residual microscopic disease, with consideration of targeted agents appropriate for the non‑V600E BRAF mutation.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases (3–5 cm) in the setting of a right T3N1 colon cancer and elevated CEA (780 ng/mL). Despite bilobar distribution, the limited number of lesions suggests that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The presence of a non-V600E BRAF D594G mutation is associated with a more indolent biology compared with V600E and does not contraindicate surgical intent. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Short peri-operative systemic therapy (recommended)
• Given the high CEA and bilobar disease, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections of all four lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to optimize margins and preserve parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Management of primary tumor
• Perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (subject to further anatomic and functional assessment).  
- Justification:  
  • Six hepatic lesions, each 2–4 cm, fall within the range commonly considered amenable to curative hepatectomy when distributed across resectable segments.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone negative).  
  • RAS wild‑type and MSS status are favorable for response to systemic therapy and for potential use of anti‑EGFR agents.  
  • High CEA (320 ng/mL) and presence of circulating tumor cells suggest aggressive biology, underscoring the need for systemic control before surgery.  
  • Definitive resectability cannot be confirmed without: hepatic segmental distribution, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures, volumetric FLR assessment, and response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – Initiate intensified chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology, achieve possible downsizing of liver lesions, and treat occult micrometastatic disease. Rationale: high CEA/CTC burden and T4 primary warrant systemic control; RAS wild‑type permits anti‑EGFR use.  
B. Restaging work‑up – After chemotherapy, obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume (CT volumetry). Evaluate vascular involvement (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery) and biliary anatomy. Rationale: precise anatomic mapping is essential to confirm resectability and plan extent of hepatectomy.  
C. Multidisciplinary decision point –  
   • If imaging shows ≥ 70 % FLR (or ≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) with clear margins achievable and no major vascular invasion → proceed to curative surgery.  
   • If FLR insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to augment FLR before resection.  
   • If disease progresses or becomes unresectable, continue systemic therapy or enroll in clinical trial.  
D. Surgical phase –  
   1. Primary colon tumor – Perform oncologic resection (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy) first if not already removed, preferably before liver surgery to avoid contamination of the hepatic field.  
   2. Liver resection – Execute an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy targeting all six metastases with negative margins (R0). Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and margins. If staged approach chosen, schedule liver resection 4–6 weeks after PVE/ALPPS once FLR is adequate.  
   3. Adjuvant therapy – Resume postoperative systemic therapy (potentially with continuation of anti‑EGFR agent) for 3–6 months, guided by pathological response and postoperative CEA/CTC trends.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
